You can only reliably see command lines for processes that are still running:

ps axho etime,cmd | sed ':a;s/^\(0*\) /\10/g;ta' | sort | less

If the process has already finished, there is no guaranteed way from this method. The closest option is to look for recently accessed executable files, but that only suggests what may have run, not the exact command line.

Examples:

find ${PATH//:/ } -type f -amin -1
find ${PATH//:/ } /home/*/bin -type f -amin -1

For about 10 seconds, it becomes even less reliable, and the provided approach only tries to filter very recently accessed files.

It won’t start because OpenSuse 12.1 uses systemd, not the classic inittab/System V startup mechanism. So adding a respawn line to inittab and running telinit q won’t launch your program.

The supported approach is to create a systemd service file in /etc/systemd/system/, for example:

[Unit]
Description=My progname service file

[Service]
ExecStart=/home/bits/MyProgram/start.myprogram

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Then run systemctl daemon-reload and systemctl start myprogname.service.

If you want it to restart automatically, add a Restart= option in the service section.

The “-” in the process field is a BusyBox-specific convention used with askfirst to start the shell as a login shell. BusyBox prefixes the shell command with “-” by putting it in argv[0], so the shell knows to behave like a login shell and may read different startup files such as ~/.profile.

So if your process won’t start, this “-” is not the reason given here; it just changes how the shell starts. The evidence only covers BusyBox inittab behavior, not other init systems or other causes of startup failure.

The process is suspending because `ant` immediately tries to read from standard input when run in the background. That causes the background job to stop.

To avoid this, don’t let it read from stdin. The supported guidance here is to run it in a way that detaches stdin, for example by redirecting input away from the terminal:

`ant -f myfile.xml < /dev/null &> foo.out &`

If it is already stopped, you can bring it back to the foreground with `fg` in the shell job control, and it should continue.

`watch` is meant to display output full-screen and update continuously, so running `watch 'cmd >> output.txt' &` is not a good fit. If you only want to run a command repeatedly in the background, use a loop like:

while true; do
    cmd >> output.txt
    sleep 2
done

This avoids the “Stopped (tty output)” problem. The provided material does not explain how to manually suspend and then bring a job to the foreground; it only shows that backgrounding `watch` in this way is unsupported and suggests replacing it with a loop.

You can’t truly send a running foreground app straight to the background without a brief stop; the terminal and shell both have to cooperate. The usual method is `Ctrl+Z` to suspend it, then `bg` to continue it in the background.

A close workaround is to bind `Ctrl+Z` so that, when there’s no text on the command line, it immediately runs `bg` for the current job. That makes the suspension time very short. If you’re using zsh, the provided `fancy-ctrl-z` function does this. To bring a background job back to the foreground, use `fg`.

If you want a Linux filesystem, use ext3:

fdisk /dev/sdb

To format an external hard drive to a Linux-compatible filesystem, the provided example uses ext4. The script shown is:

while read -r line; do
mkfs.ext4 "$line"
done < <(df -k | grep 'media' | cut -d ' ' -f 1)

This finds mounted external drive partitions under /media and runs mkfs.ext4 on each one. Be careful: this will erase data on the selected partitions.

For Linux-only use, ext4 is a good choice. The main issue is permissions: ext4 stores ownership as numeric UID/GID, so trouble can happen if your Linux machines don’t share the same user/group mappings. If they do, you should be fine.

If you want something more cross-platform and less dependent on matching UIDs/GIDs, UDF is mentioned as an option. It can be mounted with uid= and gid= options, which may help when different machines have different user databases.

Yes. The drive’s hardware doesn’t have to be “Windows” or “Linux”; an external USB hard drive can work on Linux too. The important part is the filesystem on the drive, not NFS on the file server. A consumer drive may come formatted as NTFS or FAT32, but Linux can still copy files to it if the system supports that format.

For 1 TB, speed matters: USB2 would take roughly 8–9 hours, while local SATA, eSATA, USB3, or FireWire would be much faster. If possible, connect the drive directly to the machine with the fastest available interface.

If you need one filesystem that works reasonably well across Linux, Windows, and Mac without extra drivers, UDF is a good candidate. It works out of the box on Linux 2.6.31+, Windows Vista+, and Mac OS 9+.

If you only care about Linux, the evidence doesn’t name the “best” external-drive filesystem, but UDF is at least a workable cross-platform choice. mount -t smbfs -o username=name,password=password //10.10.1.1/My-Shared-Folder /mnt/smbshare

After that, cd into /mnt/smbshare and use ls.

What this does cover: in Samba, a share may be visible but inaccessible if the guest Unix user (for example, nobody) lacks Unix filesystem permissions, or if SELinux is blocking access. For directories under /home, enabling Samba home access with:

sudo setsebool -P samba_enable_home_dirs 1

may help. For other directories, re-tag the SELinux context with:

sudo chcon -t samba_share_t /some/other/dir

If you want to find shares, you’d need to inspect the Samba configuration or browse the network from Windows.

2. Capture packets to learn the subnet, gateway, and host IPs.
3. Use nmap to scan the LAN for active machines.
4. Then check those machines for SMB/Samba shares.

This answer covers finding machines on the LAN, not directly enumerating shared folders.

That gives `%A` like `drwxr-xr-x` and `%a` like `755` or `644`.

So if you want an `ls`-like listing with octal modes, `stat` is the supported approach from this answer.

If you want uniqueness per file content instead of per path, feed `sha1sum` the file contents, not the name. Also, sha1sum is unique as long as inputs are unique, aside from extremely unlikely SHA1 collisions.

`>>` appends output to the end of an existing file.

`>` overwrites a file.

`>` redirects output to a file, overwriting it. `>>` redirects output and appends to the end of the file instead of replacing it.

With `cat`, `cat a > b` writes the contents of `a` into `b` and overwrites `b`. `cat a >> b` adds the contents of `a` to the end of `b`.

The provided material also suggests `cat a > b` is functionally similar to `cp a b` for copying a file, though `cp` would likely be more efficient.

`>` redirects output to a file, overwriting that file if it already exists. `>>` redirects output to a file, appending to the end instead of overwriting.

With `cat`, the closer related redirection is `<`, which gives a command its input from a file. So instead of `cat data | sed ...`, you can often write `sed ... < data`. That avoids starting an extra `cat` process.

In bash, `<` and `|` both affect standard input, but in different ways.

`<` connects a file to a command’s standard input.

`|` connects one command’s standard output to another command’s standard input, using an anonymous pipe.

So `|` is not “redirecting input to a program” in general; it passes output from one command to the next. Also, piping creates a subshell, while input redirection from a file does not.

In bash, use a pipeline when the output of one command should be the input of another:

If you need multiple commands to feed one command, group them first:

For input from command output as a file-like argument, bash process substitution works:

grep bar <(echo $'foo\nbar\nbaz')

Your example `command < (command2 | grep pattern)` is not the usual form; the supported form is process substitution with `<(...)`, not `< (...)`.

Use a small Python filter based on PyPdf: it splits each booklet page into two halves, reverses the second half, and writes a normal 1-up PDF.

Save this as unbook, make it executable, then run:
unbook <book.pdf >1up.pdf

Script:
#!/usr/bin/env python
import copy, sys
from pyPdf import PdfFileWriter, PdfFileReader
input = PdfFileReader(sys.stdin)
output = PdfFileWriter()
second_half = []
for i in range(0, input.getNumPages()):
    p = input.getPage(i)
    q = copy.copy(p)
    (w, h) = p.mediaBox.upperRight
    p.mediaBox.upperRight = (w/2, h)
    q.mediaBox.upperLeft = (w/2, h)
    if i % 2 == 0:
        p.rotateClockwise(180)
        q.rotateClockwise(180)
        output.addPage(p)
        second_half.append(q)
    else:
        output.addPage(p)
        second_half.append(q)
second_half.reverse()
for q in second_half:
    output.addPage(q)
output.write(sys.stdout)

The page order may vary depending on how the booklet was made.

Use packet marking plus a separate routing table for the marked traffic. Mark the desired port in mangle/OUTPUT, SNAT it to the wlan0 address, then add a rule that sends marked packets to a routing table whose default route points to wlan0.

Example:

iptables -t mangle -A OUTPUT -o eth1 -p tcp --dport 443 -j MARK --set-mark 1
iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o wlan0 -p tcp --dport 443 -j SNAT --to 192.168.0.2

Then:

echo "200 wlan-route" >> /etc/iproute2/rt_tables
ip route add default via 192.168.0.1 dev wlan0 table wlan-route
ip rule add fwmark 0x1 table wlan-route

The source may otherwise be dropped by rp_filter; the safer fix is the separate routing table.

In ATT ksh (ksh88/ksh93) and zsh, the last command in a pipeline runs in the parent shell. In bash and several others, all commands in the pipeline run in a subshell. That difference can affect variables and loop behavior.

A common workaround is to put the rest of the script in a block fed by the pipeline:

command | {
  while IFS= read -r VAR1; do
    many.commands using "$VAR1"
  done
}

If your ksh loop runs only once, upgrading to a non-buggy version is the best fix. Bash is not a drop-in replacement for ksh.

There aren’t two separate passwd files here. The issue described is with /etc/passwd, not “passwd-”.

The accepted explanation says the file was edited with Windows line endings, so root’s shell entry became /bin/bash␍ instead of /bin/bash. That means authentication can succeed, but login fails when sshd tries to start the shell.

So the closest guidance is: /etc/passwd must be fixed to use normal Linux line endings (LF only). To recover, you need root access or physical access to edit /etc/passwd and remove the stray CR character.

If you mean /etc/passwd versus /etc/passwd-, /etc/passwd- is typically a backup or alternate copy of the passwd file, not the active account database. The active file is /etc/passwd, which uses colon-separated fields like username, password field, UID, GID, GECOS, home directory, and shell.

The provided evidence only explains the format of /etc/passwd and notes that the password itself is often not stored there on modern systems. It does not define /etc/passwd- specifically. So the closest supported guidance is that /etc/passwd is the real system file, while /etc/passwd- is likely a backup copy created by some tools.

Because each account has its own entry and its own salted password hash. Even if root and your user use the same plaintext password, the stored encrypted strings will usually differ because the hash generation includes additional factors like the user/account-specific salt. So it’s not necessarily different algorithms; it’s different hashes for different users.

Yes, that’s normal. `/etc/shadow-` is a backup of `/etc/shadow`. It’s created by user-management tools like `passwd`, `useradd`, and `vipw` so the last change to the user database can be reverted if needed. You may also see similar backups like `/etc/passwd-`, `/etc/group-`, and `/etc/gshadow-`.

There isn’t a simpler built-in way to move a file and automatically update all symlinks that point to it. The approach you described is the right one: get the link target, move the file, then recreate or update the symlinks.

If you want existing links to keep the same name but point to the new file, use `ln -f` to overwrite them. If you also want the symlink names to change to match the new target name, then your planned sequence is correct.

You can do it with a fish function that moves each file and then creates a symlink back at the original location:

function lnmv
    set dest_dir $argv[1]
    set files $argv[2..-1]

    for f in $files
        set dest $dest_dir/$f
        mv -- $f $dest
        and ln -s -- $dest $f
    end
end

This supports moving multiple files. It doesn’t explicitly re-target all existing symlinks that already point to the file; it just moves the file and leaves a symlink in its old place.

Yes. A symlink’s stored target is the path text of its target, and whether it’s stored “fast” in the inode or “slow” elsewhere is just how the filesystem stores that text. That does not make symlinks auto-update when the target file moves.

To move a file and have symlinks point to the new location, you must locate and update the symlinks yourself (for example, recreate or edit them). There’s no general automatic retargeting described here.

Reaping zombie processes removes the zombie entry, but based on the provided information, zombies themselves do not consume system resources because they have already deallocated memory. So the evidence suggests there is no resource impact to worry about from zombies. It does not say anything else about side effects of reaping beyond that.

Reaping a zombie has no impact on CPU, memory, open files, or other runtime resources, because a zombie is already dead and holds only a process-table entry. Reaping just removes that entry and lets the parent collect the child’s exit status. The main impact of not reaping is that zombie entries can accumulate and clutter the process table until the parent calls wait or exits.

If the block you want to remove is between two patterns, use sed to delete the matching range:

sed '/START_PATTERN/,/END_PATTERN/d' file

This removes every line from the first line matching START_PATTERN through the first subsequent line matching END_PATTERN, inclusive.

If you want to compare two files after removing those blocks, apply the same command to both files and then diff the results:

diff <(sed '/START_PATTERN/,/END_PATTERN/d' fileA) <(sed '/START_PATTERN/,/END_PATTERN/d' fileB)

This keeps lines starting with report, -th, or -to and removes the rest.

If you want a backup of the original file:

sed -i'.bak' -e '/^\(report\|-t\(h\|o\)\)/!d' your_file

This will create your_file.bak.

Use sed to match the first pattern, append the next line, then delete both:

sed -e '/pattern here/ { N; d; }'

This removes the matching line and the line immediately after it only when they occur together.

kill -9 (SIGKILL) normally cannot be ignored, but it is delivered asynchronously and may not take effect right away. If the process is stuck in kernel code or in an uninterruptible sleep, it can appear “unkillable” until that system call returns.

The classic case is a process in state D (uninterruptible sleep), often because of I/O, especially a hung NFS server. In that situation, even kill -9 may seem to hang.

Also, root cannot send a fatal signal to PID 1. Otherwise, if you own the process and it’s not setuid/setgid, kill -9 should work once the process is able to receive the signal.

If `kill -9 <pid>` isn’t working, the process may be in `D` state (uninterruptible sleep), which cannot be killed. Check with:

`ps -o cmd,stat -p <pid>`

If the `STAT` column shows `D`, that’s likely the cause. If it’s not `D`, then more details about the process and what it’s doing would be needed to narrow it down.

`kill -9` should work if you have permission to signal the process. If it seems not to work, the usual reasons are:

- you don’t have permission, unless you’re root or it’s your own non-setuid/non-setgid process
- the process is stuck in uninterruptible sleep (often shown as state `D`), usually inside a system call
- in that case, even `SIGKILL` is delayed until the kernel call returns
- there’s one special exception: even root cannot kill PID 1

So if the process is in a bad kernel/system-call wait, it may look unkillable until that wait ends.

Some space is intentionally reserved by default, so `df` shows less than the full capacity even when the filesystem looks empty. The main purposes are:

- to leave space for root-owned processes and rescue actions
- to keep the filesystem from becoming too full, because performance and fragmentation can get much worse above about 95% full

If it’s just a long-term archive with few changes, this reserved space may not matter much. You can reduce it with `tune2fs -m`.

Some space can be used by filesystem metadata and by files that are logically large but physically sparse. Sparse files have zero-filled regions that don’t take disk blocks until written; copying them with tar can cause those holes to be filled, increasing used space. That explains why an “empty-looking” filesystem can still show usage, and why usage can grow after backup/restore.

Some filesystem space can appear used if the filesystem or partition is corrupted. In that case, file sizes and free-space reporting may be wrong until the filesystem is checked with fsck. The guidance here is to identify the root disk with df -h, then boot from recovery or a live disk and run fsck on the correct device. It also suggests copying off logs first if possible. It does not support that dropping caches would erase bash history or other files; the closest explanation given is filesystem corruption.

The 129 MB “used” space is likely normal filesystem overhead, not files you copied. On ext4, some space is reserved for metadata such as inodes, journal, superblock backups, and alignment. The thread also notes that `dumpe2fs` can be unreliable on a mounted partition, so its inode-size output may be wrong or outdated.

If you want to verify it, unmount the SD card and check it again with `dumpe2fs`. If the filesystem is small, the fixed ext4 metadata can look like a large chunk of used space.

The 129 MB “used” space can be normal with ext4, especially when lazy inode-table initialization is used. The filesystem may not have finished zeroing inode tables in the background yet, and that space can still appear allocated or uninitialized. The main point is that the zeros are there to prevent old garbage from being treated as valid inodes by e2fsck. If the background initialization is interrupted, the filesystem can still mount, but e2fsck may later have to do recovery and may put invalid recovered files in /lost+found.

If you want, I can also explain how this relates to ext4 reserved space and why SD cards often show less free space than expected.

That’s expected for ext4. `df` does not scan every file; it reads filesystem metadata, especially the superblock, which tracks total and free blocks. So after `mkfs.ext4`, the filesystem can still show some “used” space because ext4 reserves space for metadata and for the root user, and there may also be formatting overhead. If you want to know what the 129 MB represents exactly, the closest supported guidance is to check ext4’s reserved blocks and metadata rather than expecting the card to be completely empty.

`df` is being expanded as an alias when it appears as the first command in the alias definition, which creates an alias loop. That’s why `alias df 'printf "\n"; df -hP | column -t'` fails, while `alias df 'df -hP | column -t'` does not trigger the same loop in that context.

The workaround is to prevent alias expansion by using the full path or escaping the command name, for example:

`alias df 'printf "\n"; /bin/df -hP | column -t'`

or

`alias df 'printf "\n"; \df -hP | column -t'`

This evidence does not explain the `free_space + used_space != total_size` question; it only covers the alias loop behavior.

`df` reports filesystem block counts from metadata, not by summing file sizes. On ext4, the superblock stores the total number of blocks/inodes and how many are free, so `used_space` and `free_space` are calculated quickly.

The reason `free_space + used_space` may not exactly equal `total_size` is that the filesystem also has metadata and reserved space, so not all blocks are counted as user-available space.

Nothing is wrong with df itself. The issue is that HTML collapses whitespace and newlines, so a multi-line shell variable displayed directly in HTML can appear as one line. The guidance supported here is to wrap the output in preformatted text, for example: printf "
%s
\n" "$STORAGE" >> file.html If you want nicer presentation, generate an HTML table instead of plain text.

Yes—at least for ext3, decreasing the reserved block count may not change `df` output the way you expect. The total blocks shown by `df` still includes reserved blocks, and if the filesystem is already full, “Used” can equal the total while “Available” stays 0. That means the reserved blocks are effectively already in use. On a root filesystem, this is not surprising because many files are owned by root.

No. `df` is meant to report disk free space from filesystem metadata, so it can differ from `du`, which sums file sizes in a directory tree. `df` is faster and shows the whole disk/partition; `du` is for a specific directory or files. If the numbers don’t match, that can be normal because they measure different things.

Use `find` with boundary files created at the start and end of the range:

```sh
touch -t 201112220000 start
touch -t 201112240000 stop
find / -newer start \! -newer stop
```

If the files are named by date like /year/month/date.db, a simple script can iterate day by day from a start date to an end date, formatting each date into the matching path and echoing it if the file exists.

Example:

#!/bin/bash
STARTDATE="$1"
ENDDATE="$2"
day=0

while [ "$DATE" != "$ENDDATE" ]; do
    DATE=`date --date="$STARTDATE + $day days" +%Y/%m/%d`
    if [ -f "$DATE.db" ]; then
        echo "$DATE.db"
    fi
    day=$(($day+1))
done

This supports a call like:

It does not directly cover arbitrary systemwide file creation dates, only files stored in this date-based directory structure.

2. Concatenate those lsmod outputs into one file, removing duplicate header lines.
3. Manually add any extra modules you want to keep.
4. In the kernel source tree, run:

make LSMOD="lsmod.txt" localmodconfig

This makes localmodconfig use your saved module list, so the custom kernel supports multiple hardware boxes.

A custom kernel is typically built to change compile-time options, include debugging info, remove unused parts, replace or add patches/modules, or for learning and experimentation. It can also be needed in special cases like embedded systems or when adding custom system calls. 

It’s not usually built for speed; with modern compilers, that benefit is often overstated. In many cases, most “unnecessary” parts are modules, so the practical gain may be small. 

If you want to build one, the usual reason is to customize the kernel for your system’s needs rather than expecting a big performance boost.

To build a kernel, download the source, then run `make menuconfig && make bzImage modules && make modules_install`, and copy the new kernel image to the right place for your distribution. Writing kernel code is much harder than building it. For learning, look for Linux kernel programming resources, such as “Linux Kernel Module Programming Guide.” If you care about the whole system setup, the LFS site also covers kernel compilation.

You can build the kernel anywhere, even in your home directory. Only install targets write outside the build tree.

A typical flow is:

cd some_directory
tar -xjvf linux-<version>.tar.bz2
cd linux-<version>
make mrproper menuconfig
make -j$(grep -c processor /proc/cpuinfo) bzImage modules

If you want to install modules and the kernel to a mounted target volume like /mnt:

INSTALL_MOD_PATH=/mnt INSTALL_PATH=/mnt/boot make modules_install

That copies the kernel image to /mnt/boot and modules to /mnt/lib/modules/<version>.

If you build a monolithic kernel, you can just copy vmlinux or bzImage to your intended volume and configure your boot manager. Booting it may still require handling initramfs and bootloader setup.

If you want the output of one command to become input to another in Bash, place the redirection on the command that should receive the input, using a pipeline or process substitution.

Examples:
`command1 | command2`
`grep bar <(echo $'foo\nbar\nbaz')`

`(command1; command2 | command3; command4) | command5`

`command < file`

If you store the command in a variable, the redirection and pipe won’t be interpreted when you later run `$VER_URXVT`; it just becomes plain text. The supported approach here is to execute the stored string with `eval`:

```bash
VER_URXVT='urxvt -help 2>&1 | head -n 2'
echo $VER_URXVT
eval $VER_URXVT
```

So the redirection stays inside the command string, and `eval` makes the shell parse and run it.

`find` doesn’t take `/my/directory/*txt` as “files matching a pattern”; it treats that as a path, so the shell expands it first. If nothing matches, `find` gets a literal non-existent argument and prints the error.

Use `find` with a directory plus `-name` instead:

`find /my/directory/ -type f -name "*txt" -mtime +31 -ls`

If you only want files directly in that directory, add:

`-maxdepth 1`

So:

`find /my/directory/ -maxdepth 1 -type f -name "*txt" -mtime +31 -ls`

This can happen because of a race condition. The file may not exist when `cp` checks, but another parallel `cp` (or similar process) creates it before the actual create/overwrite step. Then `cp` gets `EEXIST` even with `-f`. The same kind of issue can happen with `mkdir -p` or other create-if-missing operations. The supported fix is to avoid concurrent creation of the same file, for example by using `flock` or otherwise serializing the script steps.

If you want to sort files into folders by date, the supported approach is to loop over the files, read each file’s timestamp, create a folder from that value, and move the file there.

For example, using file modification date on macOS:

for file in *; do
    dir="$(stat -t %Y%m%d%H%M%S -f %Sm -- "$file")"
    mkdir -p "$dir"
    mv -- "$file" "$dir/$file"
done

On Linux/GNU systems, a similar loop uses GNU stat:

for file in *; do
    dir="$(stat -c %Y -- "$file")"
    mkdir -p "$dir"
    mv -- "$file" "$dir/$file"
done

If you need the folder name in a prettier date format, you can reformat the timestamp with date.

```sh
do

    if [ -e "$mp4" ]
    then
        touch --reference="$avi" "$mp4"
    fi
done
```

On Linux, “executable” is mostly about a file permission bit, not the file extension. A file can be executable if it has the execute bit set.

There are two common cases:
- Binaries: compiled files with a format like ELF. The kernel knows how to load and run them.
- Scripts: plain text files with a shebang like #!/bin/bash. The kernel runs the interpreter named there, passing the script to it.

So compilation and linking still matter for binaries: they turn source code into machine code and combine needed pieces into a runnable format. Scripts are also “executed,” but by an interpreter rather than directly by the CPU.

Portability is limited because binaries depend on CPU architecture and library versions.

`find /my/directory/ -type f -name "*txt" -mtime +31 -ls`

If you don’t want files in subdirectories, add `-maxdepth 1`:

`find /my/directory/ -maxdepth 1 -type f -name "*txt" -mtime +31 -ls`

There isn’t really a need to pre-check with `ls`; the harmless “No such file or directory” comes from using `find` incorrectly with a globbed path.

A daemon is more than just “running in the background.” From the evidence, key daemon properties are:

- no controlling terminal
- its STDIN/STDOUT/STDERR are redirected away from the starting terminal
- its parent process is set to init
- it is a process group leader

A process started with `&` is only put into the shell’s background; that does not necessarily give it those daemon properties. So `&` is not the same as daemonizing.

The provided material only covers the `&&` vs `;` difference when backgrounding commands: `&&` runs the second command only if the first succeeds, while `;` always runs the second. It also notes that `sleep` can fail if interrupted, and that fork/exec can fail.

It does not explain daemonizing versus using `&`. Closest guidance: `&` only backgrounds the job in the shell, while daemon behavior is not covered here.

Running with `&` just tells the shell to start the job in the background. It does not, by itself, make the program independent of the shell.

A daemon is a program designed to run as a long-lived service, typically detached from the terminal and not tied to the shell session. In the evidence, the key difference is that a background job can still be killed when the parent shell exits because it receives SIGHUP. `nohup` changes that by making the program ignore SIGHUP.

So `&` means “background job,” while “daemon” implies “detached service that keeps running.” The evidence doesn’t fully describe all daemon details, but it does support that a daemon is more independent than a simple `&` job.

`command` runs a command and lets its output appear as normal shell output.

`$(command)` is command substitution: the shell runs `command`, captures its standard output, and replaces `$(command)` with that text in the surrounding command line.

So the practical difference is that `command` executes something, while `$(command)` uses the output of that execution as data. If `command` prints multiple words or lines, `$(command)` inserts them into the shell’s parsing context, which can change how they’re split or interpreted.

`command` runs the command itself.

`$(command)` runs the command first, captures its output, and substitutes that text into the surrounding command line.

So practically:
- `command` = execute it
- `$(command)` = use its output as data in another command

Example: `echo $(date)` prints the output of `date`.

`command` runs the command itself.

`$(command)` runs the command in a subshell, captures its output, and replaces `$(command)` with that output in the surrounding command.

So the practical difference is: plain `command` executes something; `$(command)` uses what it prints as text input to another command. `$(...)` can also be nested, unlike backticks.

If you mean these ways to run a shell script:

- `bash script`
- `chmod +x script` then `./script`
- `./script` after adding `#!/bin/bash`

the main difference is how the script is started.

`bash script` explicitly runs the file with bash.

`./script` runs it as an executable file, so it must be marked executable and usually have a shebang line to tell the system which shell to use.

Both run the script in a new process, so variables set inside the script do not affect the calling shell.

There are three common cases:

1) `./script` or `/path/to/script`
- Runs the script as a separate process.
- Uses the script’s shebang if present.
- Changes inside the script (like variables or `cd`) do not affect your current shell.

2) `. script` or `source script`
- Runs the script in the current shell.
- Any variables/functions it defines stay available afterward.
- A `cd` inside it changes your current directory.
- `.` is not the same everywhere; `source` is the more widely recognized form in shell-related shells.

3) `/bin/sh script`
- Explicitly runs the script with `/bin/sh`, ignoring a different shebang.
- Can fail or behave differently if the script needs bash or another interpreter.

Use `source`/`.` when you want the script to affect the current shell; otherwise use normal execution.

If you mean `bash script.sh`, `bash < script.sh`, and `bash -s < script.sh ...`, the main difference in the evidence is `-s`.

`bash script.sh` runs the file named `script.sh` as the script.

`bash < script.sh` feeds the file on standard input; bash may treat extra words after the redirection as filenames, which can fail.

`bash -s < script.sh foo bar` tells bash to read commands from standard input and treat `foo bar` as positional parameters. That’s the point of `-s`: it lets you pass arguments when the script is read from stdin.

`cd` changes the current working directory, and that directory is a property of a process. If `cd` were a separate program in `/bin`, it would run in its own process, change its own working directory, then exit. Your shell would still be in the old directory. That’s why `cd` has to be built into the shell rather than being an external file.

`cd` isn’t located as a standalone program in the usual sense. It’s a shell built-in command, because changing the current working directory must happen in the shell process itself. When you type a command, your terminal’s shell receives it and runs it. In interactive mode, it behaves much like running commands from a script. The shell may be bash in both cases. A script is executed as a new process, so changes made inside it, like setting a variable, do not affect the calling shell.

When you type a simple external command in a shell, the shell typically creates a child process and then runs the command there with execve. Built-in commands are handled directly by the shell. If you trace only the shell process, you may see just the execve from the child, because the fork/clone happened in a process you are not following. To see the process-creation calls too, trace child processes as well, for example with strace -f -e trace=process bash -c 'ls; :'. The extra : helps force bash to fork instead of just execveing the single command directly.

The fix shown is to search for the process more carefully and exclude `single-instance` and daemon processes:

`ps -fp $(pgrep -d, "$1") egrep -v "single-instance|daemon" | grep $1`

Public key SSH access and `su` are separate.

If `user_A` has their public key in `user_B`’s `authorized_keys`, then `user_A` can log in as `user_B` with:

`ssh user_B@localhost`

Whether `user_A` can then use `su` is controlled by PAM / local system policy, not by SSH keys. So SSH keys do not by themselves grant `su` rights. Private keys are not shared.

To make `su -` consult `/etc/security/access.conf`, add this line to `/etc/pam.d/su`:

`session required pam_access.so`

This makes `su` use the access rules from `/etc/security/access.conf` by default, so only the users allowed there can be switched to.

You can allow only that exact switch in /etc/pam.d/su by adding these lines under pam_rootok.so:

auth  [success=ignore default=1] pam_succeed_if.so user = martin-test
auth  sufficient                 pam_succeed_if.so use_uid user = martin

This makes `su - martin-test` from `martin` succeed without a password, while other `su` cases follow the normal checks.

If you prefer a group-based rule, `pam_succeed_if.so` can also allow members of a specific group to `su` without a password, but that is broader than a single-user exception.

```bash
counter=0

do

    if [[ counter -gt 3 ]]

        path="${REPLY#* }"
        rm -v -- "$path"
    fi
```

`for file in *.mp4\?token*; do mv --no-clobber "$file" "${file%%\?*}"; done`

This matches files like `63018933.mp4?token=...` and renames them to `63018933.mp4`. The `${file%%\?*}` part strips the `?` and anything after it.

A shell loop can do this by grouping files in lexicographic order, detecting when the non-numeric part changes, then assigning names like 1_1.txt, 1_2.txt, etc. The suggested pattern is:

current=
numbers=
i=0
for x in *.txt ''; do
  stem=${x%.*}
  n=${stem##*[!0-9]}
  stem=${stem%$n}
  if [ "$stem" != "$current" ]; then
    for k in $(printf '%s\n' $numbers | sort -n); do
      y=${i}_${k}.txt
      echo mv "$current$k.txt" "$y"
    done
    current=$stem
    numbers=$n
    i=$((i+1))
  else
    numbers="$numbers $n"
  fi
done

They’re not really “files” with those sizes; the size reflects how much filesystem space is allocated to them. The evidence explains that files are stored in fixed-size blocks, and a small file still takes one whole block. So a 1-byte file can use 4 kB if the block size is 4 kB.

That same idea is the closest explanation here: `.` and `..` are directory entries, and directories are stored as files too. Their apparent sizes can reflect the blocks allocated to hold directory entries, not just the few bytes you might expect from their names.

`.` is the directory itself, and `..` is its parent directory. Like any directory, they store entries mapping names to inode numbers. Their size reflects how much space the directory file occupies on disk, not “content” in the usual sense.

So `.` being 4 kB is just the minimum directory block size on that filesystem. `..` being 12 kB means the parent directory currently needs more space for its entries. Directory size can grow as files are created, and it usually does not shrink automatically when files are removed.

They’re directory entries. A directory’s reported size is the space needed to store its entries, and “.” and “..” are always present. “.” refers to the directory itself, and “..” refers to its parent. The 4 kB and 12 kB values are just the filesystem’s allocated sizes for those directories, not the sizes of the names themselves. The exact numbers can vary by filesystem and block size, but small directories are often one block or a few blocks in size.

Putting things other than /home on separate partitions is mainly for isolation and manageability. Separate partitions can make it easier to back up, restore, move, or reinstall parts of your data independently.

But nested mount points under /home can be awkward: /home must be mounted before anything inside it, and unmounted after everything inside it. If /home isn’t available at boot, the deeper mounts won’t appear either. If a subpartition isn’t mounted and you write into its directory, those files can seem to disappear once it is mounted.

A Linux permission string can be read like this:

- First character: file type
  - `-` = regular file
  - `d` = directory
- Next 3 characters: owner permissions
- Next 3: group permissions
- Last 3: world/others permissions

For example:
- `-rwxr-xr--` = file; owner can read/write/execute, group can read/execute, world can read
- `drwx------` = directory; owner has full access, group and world have none

If you have a specific permission string, I can decode the exact file/directory type and access for owner, group, and world.

A file/directory entry has three permission classes: user (owner), group, and other (“world”). “Other” means any account that is neither the owner nor in the file’s owning group.

A process uses user permissions if its UID matches the file owner; otherwise, if any of its group IDs match the file’s group, it uses group permissions; otherwise it uses other permissions.

So to identify access:
- user: permissions for the owner account
- group: permissions for accounts in the owning group
- world/other: permissions for everyone else

This also applies to files and directories. The evidence does not provide the exact permission bits for a specific file, only how to interpret them.

A Linux permission string tells both file type and access for user/group/others.

For example: `-rwxr-x---`
- First character: file type
  - `-` = regular file
  - `d` = directory
- Next 3 chars: owner permissions
- Next 3: group permissions
- Last 3: others/world permissions

Each set uses:
- `r` = read
- `w` = write
- `x` = execute
- `-` = not allowed

So `-rwxr-x---` means:
- regular file
- user: read/write/execute
- group: read/execute
- world: no access

The provided material also mentions checking effective access for a given user by comparing the user’s UID/GIDs against the file’s mode, ownership, and group, but it does not give a direct one-command answer for identifying file type and permissions.

```bash
while true
do
    case "${1-}" in
        -in)
            infile="${2-}"
            shift 2
            ;;
        -out)
            outfile="${2-}"
            shift 2
            ;;
        *)

done

```

- `.` means a candidate prime failed a simple primality test.
- `+` means a long primality test succeeded.
- `^` means GPG is trying a candidate generator.

The kernel headers under `asm-generic` are mostly generic, portable fallback versions written in C until an architecture-specific version exists. Architecture-specific versions live under `arch/<arch>/include/asm`. Headers under `include/linux` are the Linux-wide kernel headers, while `include/asm-generic` provides common defaults that can be reused by architectures. For `syscalls.h`, there can be both an `include/linux` version and an `asm-generic` version because one is the general kernel-side header and the other is the generic fallback used when no arch-specific one is provided.

The kernel header definitions are implemented in the header files themselves, and `make headers_install` just installs them for userspace use. You can’t include two headers with the same path at once; only one version will be found from the include search path.

If you need newer definitions, install that header set outside the normal include directories and compile with `-I` so it takes precedence. If the code uses new kernel-only features, make sure those parts can be disabled or won’t run on the older kernel.

If you literally ran `mv /tmp/folder/* /*`, the shell expanded both wildcards before `mv` ran.

`/tmp/folder/*` became every non-hidden item in `/tmp/folder`.
`/*` became every non-hidden item in the filesystem root (`/`), such as `/bin`, `/etc`, `/home`, `/tmp`, etc.

So `mv` was asked to move all items from `/tmp/folder` into the root directory. That would either:
- move files/directories into `/`, or
- if names collided with existing root entries, overwrite/replace depending on the situation and permissions.

It did not mean “move everything to some folder named `*`”; it meant “move into `/`.”

It would have tried to move everything from /tmp/folder/ into the root directory /.

Since the command used `*`, it expands to all visible names in `/tmp/folder`, so each item would be moved to `/*` — i.e. into `/`. That can overwrite or collide with existing top-level files and directories if names match, and it can badly disrupt the system. Hidden files in `/tmp/folder` would not be matched by `*`.

The evidence provided is about `/var/tmp`, not this `mv` command, so this is the closest supported interpretation.

It would have moved everything it could in `/tmp` into `/`, not just `/tmp` itself. So files and directories from `/tmp/folder/*` would likely have ended up at the root of the filesystem as `/*`, including ordinary files, and possibly breaking things by overwriting existing paths if names collided.

It would not safely preserve special `/tmp` uses like open files, pipes, sockets, or other live handles. Those are typically still held open by running programs, so copying/moving the directory contents doesn’t transfer the live state. The practical guidance given is that for `/tmp`, especially on systems with X or screen sessions, the safe recovery is usually to reboot rather than try to copy it live.

An interactive shell is one that reads from a terminal and lets you type commands. A login shell is the shell started at login. A shell can be both interactive and login, either one, or neither.

Use cases:

- Login: startup settings for a user session.

An interactive shell is one you use directly; it reads input from the terminal. A non-interactive shell runs a command or script and does not wait for your input.

A login shell is the first shell started when you log in for a session, such as on a text console, through SSH, or with su -. It commonly reads profile files like /etc/profile and ~/.profile (and ~/.bash_profile in bash).

A non-login shell is any shell that is not started as the first login shell. A common case is starting a shell from inside another shell; that is usually interactive but non-login.

Use cases:
- Interactive login: initial session setup, environment variables
- Interactive non-login: working in an already-open shell
- Non-interactive non-login: running scripts or remote commands

A symbolic link doesn’t contain separate file contents; it stores a path to its destination. To view that target directly, use `readlink` if available.

A symbolic link stores a path to the target, not the file contents. If you want to see what it points to, use `ls -l` and read the `->` part; that shows the destination path, including a relative one if it was created that way.

If you want a link that still refers to the same file even if the original location changes, a hard link is the closest match. A hard link is another name for the same inode, so it behaves like the same file. Hard links usually don’t work across filesystems and generally can’t be made to directories.

To copy the symbolic link itself rather than the file it points to, use a tool that does not dereference links. The suggested option is:

`cp -d source destination`

or equivalently:

This tells `cp` not to follow symbolic links in the source. If you need to move files over a network and preserve links, packaging everything into a `tar` archive is another workable approach.

Redirections are applied left to right, not all at once.

So in `cat file1 file2 1> file.txt 2>&1`:
- `1> file.txt` makes stdout go to `file.txt`
- then `2>&1` makes stderr go to wherever stdout is pointing now, which is also `file.txt`

If you reverse them as `2>&1 > file.txt`, then stderr is first tied to the original stdout, and only afterward stdout is moved to `file.txt`. That leaves stderr still going to the terminal.

So the “upset” order is just the shell processing redirections in sequence.

So:
- `command 2>&1 >somefile` sends stderr to the current stdout first, then changes stdout to the file, leaving stderr on the terminal.
- `command >somefile 2>&1` sends stdout to the file first, then makes stderr go to the same place as stdout, so both go to the file.

If you’re seeing a rare mismatch, the supported guidance here is to check the exact order of redirections.

Yes. If `df`, `ls`, or `umount` hang on an NFS mount, that usually means the client is waiting on the server or timing out. The supported ways to deal with it are:

- on older kernels with `intr`, kill the waiting processes; on newer kernels (2.6.25+), `kill -9` works

The closest ways to reduce the impact are:
- Use `autofs` instead of keeping NFS mounts permanently mounted.
- Mount with `soft` if you want requests to fail instead of hang, but this is not recommended because it can cause corrupted data or lost files.
- `hard,intr` is recommended for normal NFS mounts; it still waits for the server to come back.

Mount options can matter too: if the mount used nointr, signals won’t interrupt NFS file operations; intr may allow interruption, though it’s deprecated on newer kernels.

In the example, the file’s group permissions are `r--`, so the resulting mask becomes `r--` as the intersection with the directory mask `rwx`, not `rwx`.

SSH port forwarding sends traffic through an SSH connection to reach another host/port.

Local port forwarding means a port on your own machine is forwarded through the SSH server to a destination the SSH server can reach. In the example, connecting to your local port 7000 is sent via the SSH server to the Windows machine’s port 3389:

ssh -L 7000:<Windows IP>:3389 <SSH server>

Remote port forwarding is the opposite direction: a port on the SSH server side is forwarded back through SSH to a service on your local machine.

So:
- Local forwarding: your port -> SSH server -> target host/port
- Remote forwarding: SSH server port -> SSH tunnel -> your local host/port

SSH port forwarding means SSH carries traffic from one port to another over the encrypted connection.

The difference is where the traffic is forwarded from:
- -L (local forwarding): packets go from your local machine to a host/port on the remote side.
- -R (remote forwarding): packets go from the remote server side to a host/port on the local side.

So the manual’s wording is consistent: the forwarded port is the one being made available on the local host for -L, and on the remote host for -R. The key is that it’s the packets that are forwarded, not the port itself.

Local port forwarding (`-L`) listens on your local machine and sends that traffic through SSH to a remote destination. It’s used when you want to reach a remote service as if it were on your own computer.

Remote port forwarding (`-R`) does the opposite: it listens on the remote SSH server and sends that traffic back to a local service.

X uses its own independent mapping scheme for most keys, so it generally ignores kernel keymap settings. However, it does take the keyboard-specific mappings set up through udev into account.

remove mod4 = Super_L Super_R

Then load it with:

xmodmap ~/.xmodmaprc

This change lasts only for the current X session, so you need to run it again each time or add it to something like ~/.xinitrc to apply it automatically.

`sudo` and `chmod` are different things. `chmod` sets the file’s execute permission; `sudo` runs a program with different credentials.

If a user lacks execute permission, they normally cannot run the file directly. But they may still run it with `sudo`/`su` if the program is executed with credentials that do have permission.

If a user has execute permission, they can run it without `sudo` or `su` as long as no other restriction blocks it.

To make it runnable only via `sudo` or `su`, do not give that user execute permission, and configure `sudo` to run the binary as a user/group that does have it.

So “needs sudo” is not the same as “chmod did not set execute bit,” and “can run without sudo” is not always the same as “execute bit is set.”

To create files in a directory, a user needs write and execute permission on that directory. In your example, `chmod g+rw fold` gives group read/write, but not execute, so `B` still can’t create `fold/fold2` or `fold/test`. The needed fix is `chmod g+x fold` (or `chmod g+rwx fold` if appropriate).

Also, `id B` shows `gid` as B’s primary group and `groups` as all supplementary groups. Adding B to group C only affects new login sessions, so B may need to log out and back in.

If you own the file, you still may not be able to change its group unless the file system and permissions allow it. The evidence here specifically covers deletion: removing a file depends on write permission on the directory, not on the file itself. 

So for “permission denied” when trying to change a file’s group, the closest supported guidance is that ownership of the file alone is not enough; the relevant permissions are on the directory or on the operation itself. To add 512 null bytes at the start and end of the image, create a new file, write 512 zero bytes first, then copy the original image after that, then append another 512 zero bytes, and rename it back:

dd if=/dev/zero of=RISCPC.IMG.new bs=1 count=512
dd if=RISCPC.IMG of=RISCPC.IMG.new bs=512 seek=1
dd if=/dev/zero bs=1 count=512 >> RISCPC.IMG.new
mv RISCPC.IMG{.new,}

If you can use cat, another supported approach is to concatenate zero blocks before and after the image.

You don’t “unpack” a dd image with dd. If the image is of an NTFS partition, mount it as a loop device to access the files directly:

mount -o ro,loop -t ntfs disk.image /mnt/test

Then copy files or directories from /mnt/test, and unmount with umount /mnt/test.

For restoring, use dd in the same way the image was created: if it came from a partition, restore to a partition; if from an entire disk, restore to an entire disk. The destination should be the same size or larger than the image. If you restore to a smaller target, it won’t fit. If the target already has data, dd will overwrite it. The guidance here doesn’t cover safe partial restores from a specific position.

Yes. Use conv=notrunc so dd doesn’t truncate the output file. Then it will overwrite only the beginning bytes from the input file:

dd conv=notrunc if=small.img of=large.img

If you want to overwrite a specific offset, combine this with seek and/or skip, but the provided answer only covers replacing the first part of the file.

What you can access is the raw RAM contents for forensics or low-level debugging, but not a mountable filesystem. If you need something mountable, you’d need an image that actually contains a filesystem or disk partition layout.

Use grep to search file contents.

For a single directory:
grep "text" /path/to/directory/*

For recursive search:
grep -r "text" /path/to/directory/*

You can also use:
grep "text" /path/to/directory/**/*
but ** depends on the shell, and may not work everywhere.

If you want to search for text in files and then collect the contents of the matching files into one file, use grep to list matching files and pipe them to cat:

`grep -rlZ search-text some/dir/ | xargs -r0 cat > dump.test`

This searches recursively in `some/dir/`, outputs matching filenames safely, and concatenates those files into `dump.test`.

A POSIX alternative is:

`find some/dir -type f -size +0 -exec grep -q search-text {} \; -exec cat {} + > dump.test`

This is less efficient because it runs grep separately on each non-empty file.

To find files whose contents contain a string under a directory, you can use:

`cd mydir ; grep -lr apple *`

or:

`find mydir -type f | xargs grep -l apple`

These search recursively through subfolders and print the names of matching files. If you need exact matching or case-insensitive search, you’d need a variation of the command.

The likely cause was not Debian itself but a power spike: the server’s power draw increased about 15 minutes after boot, triggering the power supply’s over-current protection and causing restarts.

The spike was traced to all 74 drives starting their automatic offline S.M.A.R.T. tests at the same time. Disabling those tests with:

smartctl --offlineauto=off /dev/sdx

stopped the power spikes and the restarts for at least 20 hours.

`K` scripts are run with the `stop` argument, `S` scripts with `start`, and they run in lexicographic order. The expected format is:

`[K|S]` + `nn` + `name`

So your links should be like:

`sudo ln -s /etc/init.d/backup_files.sh /etc/rc0.d/K10backup_files.sh`
`sudo ln -s /etc/init.d/backup_files.sh /etc/rc6.d/K10backup_files.sh`

Use udev to trigger a script when the USB drive is inserted. Udev can match a filesystem label and call an external command, while the script creates the mount point and mounts the device.

A matching rule can use the label, then run:

/usr/local/sbin/udev-mount-by-label '%E{ID_FS_LABEL_ENC}'

Example script:

#!/bin/sh
mount_point="/media/$1"
current_device=$(awk '$2 == ENVIRON["mount_point"] {print $1; exit}' </proc/mounts)
if [ -n "$current_device" ]; then
  echo 1>&2 "$current_device already mounted on $mount_point"
  exit 1
fi
mount "/dev/disk/by-label/$1" "$mount_point"

This supports automatic mounting with the USB label as the mount point path. Don’t forget to unmount before unplugging to avoid data loss.

Use source-based routing (policy routing), not “route by incoming interface.”

Set up one routing table per source IP/interface, then add rules that choose the table based on the packet’s source address:

- add two tables in /etc/iproute2/rt_tables
- add routes for each interface in its own table
- add a default route via each gateway in its table
- add ip rule entries like:
  ip rule add from <IP1> table <NAME1>
  ip rule add from <IP2> table <NAME2>

This makes traffic from each source IP use its matching gateway/interface, so replies go out the same path.

You can’t route to a destination by interface alone. The system needs a next-hop host (gateway) or a directly connected network, because an interface can have many hosts on it.

What you can do is route a specific destination network through a gateway that’s reachable on that interface, for example:

ip route add 1.2.3.0/24 via 192.168.0.123 dev eth1

That sends traffic for 1.2.3.0/24 to 192.168.0.123 out eth1. If you only want a subset of traffic routed differently, this is the supported approach.

High load doesn’t necessarily mean high CPU use. In Linux, load average counts processes that are runnable or stuck waiting for disk I/O. So a system can show low CPU usage but still have high load if many processes are blocked in I/O wait.

High load can happen even when CPU and disk don’t look saturated because load is the number of processes waiting to run, not just CPU usage. In the accepted answer, the load around 4.81 means roughly 4 processes were ready but waiting for resources.

The evidence says CPU was only about 13% busy, while the HDD /dev/sdb was the busiest device, though still not fully utilized. It also suggests defunct processes may be blocking on some resource and causing other processes to wait.

`df -h` and `fdisk -l` are showing different things.

`fdisk -l` is the partition table tool, but in this case it does not support GPT, so it only sees a fake MBR entry and won’t match the real layout.

`df -h` shows mounted filesystems and their usage, not the partition table. So it can list `/dev/sda2` and others that are actually mounted.

So the mismatch is because your disk uses GPT and `fdisk` is too old or incompatible for it. Use a GPT-aware tool like `gdisk` to see the real partitions.

In df -h, the columns are related but not the same thing:

- Size = total capacity of that mounted filesystem/partition
- Used = space currently used
- Avail = free space available
- Use% = percentage used

They don’t always “correspond” exactly because of reserved blocks and filesystem overhead. So a filesystem can show some space as Used but still have a different Avail than simple subtraction suggests.

Also, /dev/sda1, /dev/sda2, /dev/sda3 are disk partitions, while /, /boot, and /home are the directories where those partitions are mounted. tmpfs is a memory-based filesystem, not a disk partition.

`df -h` and tools like `dfc` don’t use the same rounding rule.

`df -h` uses “round up” behavior, so values like 3.9G can be shown as 4.0G. `dfc` displays the value rounded to the nearest displayed precision, so it may show 3.9G instead.

So the size, used, and available figures can look inconsistent because they’re formatted differently, not because the filesystem data is different.

You can map a lock entry to a file by taking the PID and inode from /proc/locks, then searching that process’s open file descriptors for the same inode:

sudo find -L /proc/458/fd -maxdepth 1 -inum 133880 -print -exec readlink {} \;

To list all locked files:

while IFS=': ' read x x x x p x x i x; do
  sudo find -L "/proc/$p/fd" -maxdepth 1 -inum "$i" -exec readlink {} \; -quit
done < /proc/locks

If the process has exited, search /proc/*/fd instead. This is only an approximation because it matches inode only, not device number.

In `ls -l`, `s` means the setuid or setgid bit is set, depending on where it appears.

- In the user execute position: `s` means setuid + execute. The program runs with the file owner’s permissions.
- In the group execute position: `s` means setgid + execute. The program runs with the file group’s permissions.

If the execute bit is not set, you may see `S` instead, which means setuid/setgid is set but execute is not.

This does not mean “readable” or “writable”; it changes the privileges used when the file is executed.

The “s” means the file has the setuid bit set. That indicates the program runs with the permissions of the file’s owner when executed.

In `-rwsr-x---`, the `s` appears in the owner execute position, so the file is executable and setuid is enabled.

You can look up `setuid` with `man setuid` for more details.

The “s” is not a separate “other users” permission. In `ls -l`, it usually indicates a special bit combined with the execute bit:

- `s` in the user or group execute position = setuid or setgid is set, and the execute bit is also set
- `S` = setuid/setgid is set, but execute is not set

For example, `rws` means read/write/execute plus setuid.  

The normal permissions still apply only to user, group, and others. If you need per-user permissions beyond that, that’s typically done with ACLs.

df reports total allocated blocks on the filesystem, while du only sums the files it can see in directories. Another common cause is deleted files that are still open by a running process: du won’t see them, but df still counts their blocks until the process closes them.

`du` and `df` measure different things.

`du` (“disk usage”) walks a directory tree and adds up the sizes of files it can see. It reports usage for the specific directory/files you ask about.

`df` (“disk free”) checks filesystem metadata for used blocks, so it reports space for the whole disk/partition and is usually much faster.

So a big difference can happen because `du` is estimating usage from files in a directory, while `df` is reporting actual filesystem block usage for the partition, which includes things like space not visible in that directory view.

`df` reports filesystem blocks, not file sizes. If a file uses a 4K filesystem block, it counts as 4K in `df` even if the file is only 1K. `df` gets the free-block count from the kernel and multiplies by block size / 1024, so “Available” can be 0 even when `1K-blocks - Used` looks greater than 0 if the filesystem’s block granularity or reporting unit makes the simple subtraction misleading.

The closest guidance here is: don’t infer free space by subtracting `Used` from `1K-blocks`; use `df`’s `Available` field, and remember some `df` versions report in 512-byte units instead of 1024.

`df` reports space for the filesystem backing the path you ask about, and on systems with multiple devices or combined storage, the total/used/available numbers may not add up the way you expect from one partition. Because `df` counts reserved blocks in the total, but “Available” excludes them. So `1K-blocks - Used` can still be positive while `Available` is 0 if the remaining space is all reserved for root. A user-specific alternative is HOSTALIASES in glibc. You can point HOSTALIASES to a custom file, for example:

echo 'g www.google.com' >> ~/.hosts
export HOSTALIASES=~/.hosts

Then apps using gethostbyname(3) or getaddrinfo(3) can resolve g to www.google.com.

Limitations: it only works for programs using those libc functions, and it does not work for setuid/setgid/setcap programs like ping unless you are already root.

If a name is removed from /etc/hosts and isn’t registered in DNS, it cannot be resolved anymore. There’s no extra cleanup needed beyond removing the line. If you still need the name to resolve, you must keep it in /etc/hosts or register it in DNS.

Also, /etc/hosts should still contain the localhost entry, usually:
127.0.0.1 localhost
::1 localhost

So the closest alternative supported here is DNS; otherwise, /etc/hosts is the place to add local custom names.

Example:
echo 'g www.google.com' >> ~/.hosts
export HOSTALIASES=~/.hosts

Then hostnames like g will resolve to the mapped address.

Limitations: it only works for programs using gethostbyname/getaddrinfo, and it won’t work for setuid/setgid/setcap programs because the environment is sanitized. For example, ping usually won’t honor it unless you’re already root.

Use capture groups in `sed`: wrap the part you want to reuse in `\(...\)` and refer to it in the replacement with `\1`, `\2`, etc.

Example:

`sed 's/..\(.*\(..\)\)/\2\1/'`

This replaces the first two characters of each line with the last two, for lines with at least 4 characters:

`echo abcdef | sed 's/..\(.*\(..\)\)/\2\1/'`

Result: `efcdef`

So the general pattern is: match what you need, capture the reusable part, then put it back with backreferences.

Use a capture group so you can replace the matched part and keep the rest of the line:

sed -r "s/=~(.*)$/match(\1)/" <filename>

If you want to do it as two separate edits only on lines containing `=~`, put the commands in a block:

sed -re "/=~/ {
  s/=~/match(/
  s/$/ )/
}" <filename>

Your error happened because sed saw the second `s/.../.../` as part of the first command, not as a separate command.

Use `^string1^string2^` to repeat the previous command and replace the first occurrence of `string1` with `string2`. It’s equivalent to `!!:s/string1/string2/`.

You can omit the final `^` only if it is the last character on the line. In that case, the closing delimiter is optional.

So these are both valid:

`^aa^bb^`
`^aa^bb`

It substitutes only the first matching string in the previous command, not all occurrences.

The master side is the “other end” of the terminal wires: xterm reads characters from it and writes keystrokes/control sequences to it. The terminal emulator mostly just emulates the display and keyboard path; it can also change terminal settings like size, which can trigger SIGWINCH.

Double hyphens are used for actual options like `--anchored` because that follows the normal GNU-style convention for long options. A single hyphen is used for short options like `-b`.

For `find`, though, many things that look like options are really expression elements or predicates, and POSIX `find` also has true options such as `-H` and `-L`. The `-`-prefixed multi-character forms in `find` are part of its expression syntax, not “long options” in the usual sense.

So the difference is mostly about command design: long options use `--name`, short options use `-x`, while `find`’s `-name`, `-type`, etc. are expression operators rather than ordinary options.

In tar, single-character options traditionally use a single hyphen, like -b. GNU-style long options use a double hyphen, like --anchored.

The reason is historical convention: older Unix tools used short flags after one -, while newer GNU tools added long option names with -- to distinguish them from short ones. So tar -b is a short option, and tar --anchored is a long option.

`iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 992 -d localhost -m owner ! --uid-owner root -j REJECT`

So the closest supported approach is to create rules based on the process owner (UID), not the program itself.

sudo works because the sudo binary is installed with the setuid bit set and owned by root. When you execute it, it runs with root’s effective user ID, even though your real user is unprivileged. That’s why it can then perform privileged actions and why `ps` shows `sudo` running as root.

The accepted explanation also points to `setuid()` as the mechanism behind this privilege change: it sets the effective user ID of the calling process, and on Linux can also affect the real and saved IDs in the root case.

mv file.new /path/to/file

If your “list” contains the names to remove, this removes any whole line in the file that exactly matches one of those names. -F treats names as plain text, -x matches whole lines, -f reads the list file, and -v inverts the match.

This deletes all regular files recursively, including hidden ones, except file.txt.

If you need to keep multiple names, add more exclusions, for example:

find . ! -name 'file1.txt' ! -name 'file2.txt' -type f -exec rm -f {} +

A simple bash script can renumber files by shifting any filename number greater than or equal to the inserted position up by 1, while preserving extensions:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
NEWFILE=$1

for file in `ls|sort -g -r`
do
    filename=$(basename "$file")
    extension=${filename##*.}
    filename=${filename%.*}

    if [ $filename -ge $NEWFILE ]
    then
        mv "$file" "$(($filename + 1))".$extension
    fi
done
```

Yes. The supported approach is to split each GIF into frames, combine corresponding frames side-by-side with montage, then stitch the combined frames back into one GIF:

#!/bin/bash
# $1 : first gif
# $2 : second gif

mkdir first
cd first
convert $1 x%04d.gif
cd ..
mkdir second
cd second
convert $2 x%04d.gif
cd ..

for filename in first/*
do
  filename=`basename $filename`
  montage -tile 2x1 -geometry 512x512 first/$filename second/$filename concat$filename
done
convert concat* output.gif

rm -rf first
rm -rf second
rm concat*

This answers combining several layers/animations into one GIF. If you need a delay of 30 frames, the provided script does not include that; the closest supported workaround is to insert blank frames before the delayed animation.

`-exec` is only attached to the `-name .classpath` part because `-o` has lower precedence than the implicit `-a` in `find` expressions.

So this:

`find mydir -maxdepth 2 -name .project -or -name .classpath -exec echo {} \;`

is interpreted like:

`( -name .project ) OR ( -name .classpath AND -exec echo )`

That’s why only `.classpath` gets passed to `-exec`.

Use parentheses to group the names first:

`find mydir -maxdepth 2 \( -name .project -o -name .classpath \) -exec echo {} \;`

This will run `-exec` for both matches.

Use either:

or

With `\;`, `grep` runs once per file. With `+`, `find` passes as many files as possible to each `grep` call.

Main advantages: related files are grouped by purpose, so it’s easier to find configs (/etc), logs (/var/log), executables (/usr/bin), and runtime data (/var/run). That also makes administration and scripting simpler, because you can predict where to look.

Another advantage is separation of executables from data. Programs, templates, logs, and configuration live in different places, which can improve organization and may reduce the impact of some filesystem viruses compared with systems that keep more application files together.

A likely disadvantage is that application files are spread across many directories, which can feel less intuitive than “everything in one folder” and may be harder for newcomers to understand.

The main advantage of Linux’s file hierarchy is standardization across many distributions: FHS helps commands and software find files in expected places, which improves compatibility and reduces breakage. It’s also fairly well respected by most GNU/Linux distros.

The main disadvantage is rigidity and slow change: it can be hard to reach consensus on where things should go, and changing locations can break existing commands and software. Compared with other Unix-like systems, the Linux FHS is not universally followed. POSIX is much lighter here, so other systems have more flexibility but less shared directory structure.

The system doesn’t need /etc/fstab to mount the root filesystem initially. The boot loader passes the kernel a root= parameter, and the kernel mounts that partition as / before starting init.

After that, init reads /etc/fstab to mount the rest of the filesystems and apply mount options. In many setups, the root filesystem is first mounted read-only, then later remounted using the options from fstab.

So “including” the root entry in fstab is mainly for later mounting/remounting behavior, not for the first step of boot.

Without execute, you can’t use the directory path to reach files or subfolders, even if you can list the directory. Read lets you list names in the folder; write lets you create, rename, or delete entries there.

- write lets you create or delete entries
- execute lets you access/traverse the directory

A hard link is generally “smaller” in the filesystem sense: it’s just another directory entry pointing to the same inode. A symbolic link stores a path to the target, so it has a little extra data and can also point across filesystems or to directories.

On speed, the evidence doesn’t give a direct benchmark. It does imply hard links are simpler because they are indistinguishable from other directory entries, while symlinks require following a path and can break if the target moves. So if you want the closest supported answer: hard links are usually a bit more direct/simpler; symlinks are more flexible.

Hard links are generally “smaller” in the sense that they are just another name for the same inode, so there’s no separate target path to store. A symbolic link stores a path to the target, so it has a little extra overhead.

For “faster,” the evidence doesn’t compare speed directly. It does show that a hard link behaves like the same file, while a symlink resolves via its path. If you move the whole directory, a relative symlink can still work. If you need the link to keep referring to the same file no matter what happens to the original location, a hard link is the better fit, with the caveat that hard links usually don’t work across filesystems and typically can’t be made to directories.

The supported way shown here is not a direct “clone Debian” tool, but a manual migration:

1. Boot from a rescue/live disc.
2. Create the new target partitions or LVM volumes.
3. Format them.
4. Mount the new root filesystem, and mount old root somewhere else.
5. Copy the system with tar, for example:
(cd /old-root && tar --one-file-system -c .) | (cd /new-root && tar vx)
6. Chroot into the new system.
7. Update /etc/fstab, mount /proc, /sys, and /boot, then run update-initramfs -u and update-grub.
8. Reboot and verify the new root is used.

The answer recommends LVM instead of manually resizing/copying partitions.

`sed` does return an exit status, but it reflects whether `sed` ran successfully, not whether your regex matched. So a non-matching substitution still usually exits 0.

If you need to know whether a match occurred, GNU `sed` can help with `q [exit-code]`, for example:

`echo "trash" | sed '/foo/{s/f/b/;q}; /foo/!{q100}'`

This exits 100 when `/foo/` is not found.

For “did any substitution succeed anywhere in the input?”, the thread shows a more complex `hold space`/`q` approach, but that relies on GNU `sed` extensions.

sed can do this by matching the whole line and keeping only the part before the final `}`:

`sed -i 's@^\([^{]\+\)\(\.to[^{]\+\)}\s*$@\1\2@' file`

This removes a trailing unmatched `}` only on lines that contain `.to` and no `{` anywhere in the matched part. If you want to return just the matched string rather than edit the file, use the same pattern in a print-only workflow, but sed’s direct example here is for substitution in-place.

`sed` normally returns only a process exit status: 0 if it ran successfully, nonzero if there was an error. A pattern not matching is not an error, so it still exits 0.

If you only want to print the matched string, GNU `sed` can do it with a match and quit, for example:

`sed -n '/pattern/{s/.*\(pattern\).*/\1/p;q}'`

Or, if you just want to print matching lines, use:

`sed -n '/pattern/p'`

If you need `sed` to signal “matched” vs “not matched,” GNU `sed` supports `q [exit-code]`, so you can quit with a custom code after a match or after no match.

ifconfig does not discover your public IP from the internet. It reads the IP address that is already configured on the network interface in the local kernel data structures.

So the address it shows is the machine’s configured interface address, not necessarily the one “visible from the internet.” If the machine is behind NAT, the internet may see a different public IP than the one ifconfig shows.

If you want the address as seen externally, you need to query an external service (for example with curl to a “what is my IP” site).
