wget gets 403 because the server is probably checking something besides the URL, not just the file itself. The most likely causes are missing cookies, a required Referer header, or sometimes Authorization or a User-Agent check.

In the thread, the specific problem was that the server checked the referrer, so adding a referer header allowed the download. Another detail was that the server redirected through a 302 to a location that did not do the check.

For wget, try setting headers similar to your browser, especially:
- referer: --referer=URL
- user agent: --user-agent=...
- cookies: --load-cookies / --save-cookies

If it still fails, compare the exact browser request headers with developer tools.

In bash, the order is: alias first, then special builtins in POSIX mode, then functions, then builtins, then commands found via $PATH.

So `test` normally runs the shell builtin before `/usr/local/bin/test` or `/usr/bin/test`.

To run the external executable, use an explicit path like `/usr/bin/test`. To ignore aliases and functions, use `command test`. To bypass an alias only, use `\test`. You can also disable or re-enable a builtin with `enable test`.

This points to a broken $PATH, so the shell can’t find standard commands like grep, tar, cat, or even bash. The fix is to check where PATH is being set or overwritten, usually in /etc/profile and then ~/.bash_profile when you log in. Make sure PATH includes the directories where those executables live, and verify the commands are actually installed there. If a local directory executable is sometimes missed, it may also be because that directory is not included in PATH or the PATH got reset in your shell startup files.

This points to missing shared libraries rather than the executable itself being absent. If `./program` says “file not found” or does nothing while `/usr/bin` programs still work, the binary may be there but its required dynamic loader/library isn’t. The suggested check is:

`ldd ./alfresco-install.bin`

Review whether any dependencies are “not found.” If so, install the missing libraries or use a binary built for your system.

A login shell’s prompt is set by that shell’s own startup files, so if the remote account’s `.bashrc` can’t be changed, you can’t make the remote prompt colors work by changing only your local `.bashrc`.

The closest workaround described is to use SSH key `command=` in `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` to set `HOME` to a private directory, then run the original command or an interactive shell. Put your desired config files there.

For occasional use, you can also explicitly source a profile file when connecting, or run a command with `ssh user@server "…"`, and use `ssh -t` for interactive sessions.

Add `export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-1.7.0-openjdk` to the end of your home directory’s `~/.bashrc` file.

`~/.bashrc` is read when you open a new interactive terminal, so the variable will be set again automatically each time. If you edit it in a file manager, remember that `.bashrc` is hidden because the name starts with a dot; in Nautilus, press Ctrl+H to show hidden files.

After saving the file, open a new terminal and `cd $JAVA_HOME` should work without retyping the export.

Try using SSH to run a remote kill without creating another login, for example:

ssh -n remuser remhost kill -HUP -1

That may bypass the one-login-per-user limit. If that doesn’t work, you’ll need someone with access to the server to switch to your user account and run:

su remuser

Then run:

kill -HUP -1

This is the closest guidance the thread supports.

Use SSH’s escape sequence: press Enter, then type `~` followed by `Ctrl+Z`. This suspends the local SSH session so you can get back to your shell. The escape character is `~` by default and is only recognized right after Enter.

If your SSH session is stuck or dropped, the guidance given is to terminate the old `sshd` processes. One way is to find your current session PID, then kill the other `sshd` sessions, for example:

`ps -ef | grep sshd | grep -v -e grep -e root -e <your_pid> | awk '{print "sudo kill -9", $2}' | sh`

You can first run it without `| sh` to verify the PIDs.

On Linux, you can also use:

`pkill -o -u $USER sshd`

to kill your oldest SSH session, repeating until only your current session remains.

If `visudo` is blocking access, delete the lock file, usually `/etc/sudoers.tmp`, then run `visudo` again.

No. The supported approach is to wrap `ssh` in a shell script instead of relying on an alias, because if the SSH session times out the rest of the alias/script after `ssh` won’t run.

That means you can do setup before `ssh`, but you can’t rely on cleanup or “unfreezing” code afterward when the connection drops. The guidance here only covers using a wrapper script for setup/cleanup around `ssh`; it does not provide a way to recover a frozen `bash` or `vim` session after an SSH timeout.

If the SSH connection itself is hung, you generally can’t “unfreeze” bash or vim inside it. What you can do is use SSH’s escape sequence to disconnect the client without closing your terminal: press Enter, then type `~.`

This works only when SSH is ready to read an escape sequence, so it’s recognized immediately after hitting Enter. You can also change the escape character with `-e` or `EscapeChar` in ssh config.

This lets you drop the stuck SSH session and open a new one, but it doesn’t recover the frozen remote shell/editor session.

No. The session described is a network/SSH stall, not something bash or vim can “unfreeze” locally. The closest guidance here is to diagnose and fix the connection issue, e.g. test by lowering the MTU on your Mac interface (for example, `sudo ifconfig en0 mtu 1100`) and see whether `scp` or SSH still stalls. If it still stalls even at a low MTU, the problem is likely a broken network device somewhere.

Using the whole block device directly can work, especially for things like RAID, encryption, LVM, or a filesystem on top of the entire device. The main downside is safety and compatibility: the kernel and tools may scan for partitions, and if the disk later contains data that looks like a partition table, it could be misinterpreted. Also, tools like fdisk will not show anything sensible on an unpartitioned disk, and someone might accidentally write a partition table over your data. The guidance supported here is that a partition table is usually safer, even if it is not strictly necessary.

A partitionless filesystem can be simpler to manage because Linux already presents everything in one directory tree, so partitioning is not needed for “organization” by itself. The main value of partitions is practical: separating /, /home, /var/www, or other important data can make reinstalling or changing distros easier, and can isolate precious data on RAID, encrypted, or remote storage.

The evidence does not compare a true partitionless filesystem against specific partition schemes in performance terms. It does say partitioning itself does not affect performance much; filesystem choice and mount options do.

The evidence does not say you can use a disk with no partitioning. It only discusses using one root partition versus separate root and /home partitions, and it notes that Windows restore/repair media may overwrite the whole drive and won’t understand Linux filesystems. So the closest guidance is that the disk is still being partitioned in those examples, just differently.

Yes, some Linux distros can be installed without losing the data on an existing Windows partition by shrinking the NTFS partition and creating new Linux partitions in the freed space.

But the guidance here does not support using a disk completely without partitioning it. It says Linux was “even possible” to install into a Windows file system, but that is “no fun,” so the supported approach is to create partitions.

Before changing partitions, run Windows’ check disk tool and make a backup, since there is some risk.

Yes, at least for some non-boot external devices. The accepted answer says many free/open systems do not have an issue with partition tables on USB keys and SD cards, and the example shows a filesystem created directly on an SD card was mounted automatically. It also suggests the main problems are usually with some closed operating systems. If you need a bootable disk or maximum compatibility, a partition table is still the safer choice.

The provided text only shows how to copy a GPT partition table and notes that a GPT table exists on the source disk. It does not say whether partition tables are always required in general. The closest supported guidance is that if you are using GPT, tools like sgdisk can copy that partition scheme to another disk, and GUIDs may be randomized if both disks will be used in the same machine.

No. A filesystem can exist directly on a block device with no partition table, and that isn’t inherently wrong. The main limitation is that you can only have one filesystem there, with no extra partitions such as swap. It is also unlikely to be bootable, since bootloaders usually use space associated with partitions. In your case, the tool may be reporting incorrectly, or the disk may use GPT rather than a legacy PC partition table. You could verify with parted, gdisk, or by checking /proc/partitions.

You have to use `./` when running a program from the current directory because the shell doesn’t normally search the current directory for executables. `./program` explicitly means “run program in this folder.”

If you want to run a script without `./`, the directory containing it must be in your `PATH`.

Also, if the script is not executable, you need to make it executable first, for example with `chmod +x script.sh`.

You use `./` because `.` means the current directory, and files in the current directory are usually not in your `$PATH`. So `./program` tells the shell to run `program` from here. Commands like `ls` or `gcc` work without `./` because their locations are already in your `$PATH`. If you want, you can check where a command comes from with `type` or `which`.

You need `./` because the current directory is usually not included in your `PATH`. When you type just `apache2`, the shell looks only in the directories listed in `PATH`, so it won’t search `.` unless you add it. Using `./apache2` explicitly tells the shell to run the program from the current directory.

Commands meant for normal use are placed in directories on `PATH`, which is why they can be run without a directory prefix.

`./` means “the current directory.” When you type a command like `ls` or `gcc`, the shell looks for it in the directories listed in your `PATH`. The current directory is usually not in `PATH`, so a program sitting there won’t be found by name alone. `./program` tells the shell to run the executable named `program` from the current directory.

If you know the interface you want, you can get its IP address in a shell script like this:

ip="$(ifconfig | grep -A 1 'eth0' | tail -1 | cut -d ':' -f 2 | cut -d ' ' -f 1)"

This looks for `eth0`, takes that line and the next one, then extracts the address. If you need wlan or other interfaces too, this specific approach doesn’t cover that.

You can’t make a binary built against GLIBC-2.9 run on GLIBC-2.8 just by using `./`. The supported workaround is to provide the newer glibc with the program and start it with the newer dynamic linker, for example:

`LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/path/to/libs /path/to/newer/ld.so ./your-application`

That may also require bundling `libpthread` and other glibc components the app uses. Another option is running it in a chroot with the newer libc installed.

`./` means “in the current directory.” You use `./filename` when the executable is in the directory you’re currently in, but that directory is not normally included in your `PATH`. Commands like `gcc` and `ls` work without `./` because they are found in directories listed in `PATH`. 

So `./foo` tells the shell to run `foo` from the current folder. You can use `type` or `which` to see where commands in your `PATH` are located.

`./` is needed because `.` means the current directory. When you type `./filename`, you are telling the shell to run the executable named `filename` from the directory you are in now.

Commands like `gcc` or `ls` work without `./` because they are found through your `$PATH`, which lists directories the shell searches for commands. Your current directory is usually not in `$PATH`, so the shell won’t look there unless you specify `./`.

You can use `type` or `which` to see where commands in your `$PATH` are located.

You don’t need `./filename` just because it’s an executable. `./` means “run this file from the current directory.” In a script, `filename` alone works only if its directory is in your `PATH`; otherwise you must use a path like `../filename` or `./filename`.

The answer here is that the script likely needs an explicit path to the executable, especially if the current working directory is different when the script runs. The suggested fix is to get the script’s absolute directory with:

`basedir="$(dirname $(readlink -f $0))"`

then call:

`$basedir/../filename {options} {parameters} &`

This makes the path reliable even if you run the script from another directory.

Because `scriptname` is only found if its directory is in your `PATH`. `./scriptname` explicitly says “run the file in the current directory,” which is why it works when the script is not in `PATH`.

The supported fix is to call local scripts with `./` or otherwise ensure the script’s directory is in `PATH`. Adding `.` to `PATH` can work, but it’s a security risk, so the proper solution is to update the scripts to reference local executables correctly.

In sed, `./` by itself doesn’t appear in the evidence. The closest match is `/ Links: /`, which means an address filter: apply the following command only to lines matching that regular expression.

More generally, `.` in a regular expression matches any single character, and `/.../` is the delimiter used to mark a regex in sed. If you meant a different `./` usage, please share the exact command.
./ means “this directory” or “the current directory” in a file path. For example, ./script.sh refers to script.sh in the directory you’re already in.

Yes. `./script.sh` runs the script file directly, so the shell used is determined by the script’s shebang line, like `#!/bin/bash`, assuming it’s executable.

`bash script.sh` explicitly invokes `bash` to interpret the script, using the `bash` found first in your `$PATH`, which may be a different Bash version than `/bin/bash`.

So the main difference is how Bash is chosen: direct execution uses the shebang, while `bash script.sh` uses the `bash` command from your path.

`bash script.sh` starts a new Bash process and runs `script.sh` in it. `./script.sh` also runs the script as a separate program, but it uses the script’s shebang line (for example `#!/bin/bash`) to choose the interpreter.

So, if the script is a Bash script, these are usually very similar: both run it in a new process. The main difference is that `bash script.sh` explicitly uses Bash, while `./script.sh` depends on the file being executable and having a valid shebang.

This is different from `. script.sh` or `source script.sh`, which run the script in the current shell process and can affect the caller’s variables and environment.

If you can’t recover files and just want to try making the card usable again, the guidance here is to wipe it and recreate the partition table.

sudo dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/sdx

Replace sdx with your card’s device name, without a partition number.

The installation path of the executable is irrelevant. The process starts with the current directory inherited from its parent process; if you launch it from a shell, that’s usually the shell’s current directory, not the directory containing the executable.

The current directory only changes if the process calls `chdir(2)` (and has permission).

With `find`, `-regex` must match the whole path that `find` is returning, not just the filename. So if you search `.` the paths look like `./file`, but if you search `/home/adam/dir` the paths look like `/home/adam/dir/file`. Your regex has to include that prefix.

For dotfiles, the closest simpler guidance is to use `-name` instead of `-regex`, for example:

`find /whatever -name '.*[!~]'`

If you must use `-regex`, make it allow the directory prefix, such as:

`find -E /whatever -regex '(\n|.)*/\.[^/]*[^~]'`

The shell expands `*foo*` before `find` runs. If there’s a match in the current directory, `find` receives the matched filenames instead of the pattern, which changes the command. If there is no match, bash passes the literal `*foo*`.

To search for files with `find`, quote the pattern so the shell does not expand it:

`find . -name '*foo*'`

If you want non-matching globs to disappear instead of being left literal, bash has `shopt -s nullglob`, but for `find` the quoted form is the right approach.

`find` can only put `{}` at the end with `-exec ... +`. If you need extra arguments after the found files, you wrap the command in `sh -c`.

In `sh -c 'script' x a b`, `x` becomes `$0` and `a b` become `$1 $2 ...`. So `sh` plus the extra word after the script is there to give `$0` a placeholder name, while `{}` becomes the actual file list passed as `"$@"`.

The `exec` inside the shell replaces the shell with the real command, avoiding an extra process.

If your goal is to avoid matching `*.sh` at a certain level, this does not directly address that; it only explains how `find -exec ... +` works.

If you want `find` to avoid prefixing results with `./`, the supported change is to start from `*` instead of `.`:

`find * -type l -name '*.sh' -exec ... {} \;`

That makes `{}` expand without the leading `./`.

This only directly addresses the path-prefix issue, not limiting searches to “certain levels.” The provided answer does not cover depth control for `*.sh`.

`find` can’t filter by directory “level” with `*.sh` alone; that pattern only matches names. The closest supported approach is to limit traversal depth and/or prune directories, then search for shell scripts.

For example, to search only certain levels:
`find . -maxdepth 2 -name '*.sh'`

If you want to skip a specific subdirectory branch:
`find . -path './some/dir' -prune -o -name '*.sh' -print`

If you mean “don’t search deeper than a certain depth,” use `-maxdepth`.

Use `cd -` to switch to your previous directory.

If you want to refer to that location in a prompt or command, use `~ -`? More accurately, Bash exposes it as `~-`, as in `ls ~-`.

A normal user generally can’t use `chown` to change a file’s owner to someone else. On most Unix systems, `chown` is restricted so users can’t “give away” files they own; only root can do that, or the user may only change ownership within privileges they already have.

To compare two strings directly in a shell script, you can use:

`if [ "$a" = "$b" ]; then ... fi`

For the example shown, a simple exact match is:

`if [ "$(echo hello)" = "hello" ]; then echo it works; fi`

If you want a case-insensitive substring check, use `grep`:

`if echo Hello | grep -iqF hello; then echo it works; fi`

`-i` ignores case, `-q` suppresses output, and `-F` treats the pattern as a plain string.

In a C shell script, compare strings with `==` inside an `if`:

```csh
if ($f1 == $f2) then
  echo "match"
endif
```

A sample approach is to combine the two files line-by-line with `paste`, then split each pair and compare them:

```csh
#!/bin/csh

foreach i (`paste -d"-" file1 file2`)
  set f1=`echo $i | cut -d"-" -f1`
  set f2=`echo $i | cut -d"-" -f2`
  if ($f1 == $f2) then
    echo "$f1 $f2 -> match"
  else
    echo "$f1 $f2 -> \" \""
  endif
end
```

This produces matches for `A A`, `D D`, and `E E`.

- Drop everything else
- Use stateful rules for established/related connections
- Allow loopback traffic

iptables -A INPUT -i lo -j ACCEPT

Process groups and sessions are mainly for terminal/job-control behavior, not just for finding descendants quickly.

A process group determines which processes can access a controlling terminal: only the foreground process group may read/write it, and background ones may be stopped by SIGTTIN or SIGTTOU. Sessions track which process groups are attached to a terminal. Only processes in the same session as the controlling process can be foreground or background processes.

You cannot derive process groups or sessions from PPID alone, because PPID does not tell you whether related processes are in the same group or session.

A simple way is to parse `pstree -p $pid` and extract only the PIDs in parentheses:

`pstree -p $pid | grep -o '([0-9]\+)' | grep -o '[0-9]\+'`

Or with Perl:

`pstree -p $pid | perl -ne 'print "$1\n" while /\((\d+)\)/g'`

These avoid mistaking digits in command names for PIDs. If you want descendants to stay together as a group for launching a command, you can start it in its own process group, for example with:

`perl -e 'setpgid or die; exec { $ARGV[0] } @ARGV;' my_command args`

But process groups do not nest, so child processes that create their own groups won’t remain in yours.

What it does show is that this pipeline can be stopped by SIGTTIN when a process in the pipeline ends up trying to read from the terminal while the job is backgrounded relative to the tty.

Closest guidance: in a pipeline like `for ...; do cat "$i" | sort; done | more`, the loop and the commands inside it can interact with job control in a way that causes a tty read attempt, which triggers SIGTTIN. Because the `while read snack ...` is fed by a pipe, Bash runs that loop in a subshell. Any `FILES+=($snack)` done there updates only the subshell’s copy of the array, which is discarded when the loop ends. That’s why only the values added in the non-pipelined `for` loop remain.

To preserve the array, avoid the pipe and use process substitution or redirection, for example:

`while read snack; do FILES+=($snack); done < <(find /var/candy -name "chocolate_[0-9]")`

or:

`while read snack; do FILES+=($snack); done <<<"$(find /var/candy -name "chocolate_[0-9]")"`

Because in bash a command in a pipeline usually runs in a subshell. So `cat junk | while read ...; do x=55; done` changes `x` only inside that subshell, and the parent shell still has `x=1`.

When you use input redirection instead:

`while read var; do x=55; done < junk`

the loop runs in the current shell, so `x` becomes `55`.

If you want to keep the pipeline form and still use the modified variable afterward, bash can do that with `shopt -s lastpipe` in some cases, or you can group the loop and follow-up commands in braces.

A device controller is not mainly there to let one driver work across different manufacturers’ devices. Its primary role is to provide part of the interface between the processor and the device.

It usually has its own driver, separate from any driver for the attached device. The processor connects through a bus, often via a bridge on the motherboard, then to the controller, and then to the device: processor -> bridge -> controller -> device.

So the controller sits between the hardware and the processor side of the system, and the kernel/drivers communicate with the controller rather than directly with the raw device.

So `var` and `var2` are assigned in the shell itself, and `var` remains changed after the loop.

A workaround is to use another mechanism, such as a sequence plus `xargs`, for example:

`seq 2 | xargs -i{} echo dir{}/file{}`

which produces:

The closest guidance it supports is that brace expansion is a shell text-expansion feature used for generating multiple strings, while arithmetic expansion is a separate mechanism for numeric expressions. A 64-bit process on a 64-bit kernel can address vastly more memory; on x86_64 there is a current per-process limit of 128 TB of address space. This is virtual memory, not the same thing as physical RAM.

If the files were accidentally deleted, the main advice is to avoid disk writes right away, because they can overwrite recoverable data. Don’t install recovery tools immediately.

Best options supported here:
- Restore from an auto-backup created by your editor, if one exists.
- If it was a text file and you remember a unique string, try searching the disk device for it, for example:
  sudo grep -i -a -B100 -A100 'string' /dev/sda1 > file.txt

Replace /dev/sda1 with the partition where the file was stored, and 'string' with something unique from the file. You may get some extra data, but it can help recover text.

If you need exact undelete for other file types, this doesn’t fully cover that.

If the deleted files were on an ext filesystem, the supported approach here is to use extundelete from another Ubuntu system while the target partition is unmounted. If restoring a specific directory doesn’t work, try:

sudo extundelete /dev/sda1 --restore-all

This can recover files even when their names/paths can’t be linked. The answer also notes the output can be misleading, and recovery may be limited if the inodes are already lost or fragmented. If your filesystem isn’t ext, this method won’t apply.

If the files were deleted with `rm -R`, recovery is uncertain, especially on modern SSDs where TRIM may zero deleted data immediately.

You can use a shell loop with `find` to list files, sort them, and move each file only when the target directory is empty:

```bash
target="some/path with/spaces"

find . -maxdepth 1 -type f | sort -r | while IFS= read -r file; do
  counter=0
  while [ $counter -eq 0 ]; do
    if find "$target" -maxdepth 0 -empty | read; then
      mv -v "$file" "$target" && counter=1
    else
      sleep 1
    fi
  done
done
```

used to repopulate the missing directory from the other system.

After restoring the directory, some commands may still not work, and you may need to reinstall the packages that provide them. This does not directly cover generic deleted-directory recovery, but it does support restoring an accidentally deleted critical directory by copying it from a similar system.

A high load average means the run queue is long: there are more runnable processes or threads wanting CPU time than the system can immediately run. It can be higher than the number of running processes, because load is an average length of the queue, not just a count of currently running tasks. Multithreaded processes can contribute more than 1. If load is higher than the number of CPU cores, some tasks are waiting for free CPU time.

It usually means `top` saw a process in the list, but that process exited before `top` could read its details from `/proc/.../mem`. It’s more common on a busy system and is generally safe to ignore. The message itself doesn’t indicate running out of memory.

If your tags file is in proper tags database format, there are plugins that can highlight tags, such as TagHighlight or EasyTags.

They’re designed for ctags-generated databases, though, so they may not fit a free-form notes workflow directly. The closest guidance supported here is to use one of those plugins for highlighting and see whether you can disable their ctags-generation assumptions or reuse only the highlighting portion.

In sed’s basic regular expressions, most metacharacters need a backslash to be treated as special. For example, `{` and `}` must be written as `\{` and `\}` to mean repetition. Without the backslash, they’re treated as literal characters.

This is the opposite of many other regex flavors, where metacharacters are special unless escaped.

So, in this context, the characters that commonly need escaping to act as regex operators include braces and others like parentheses and `+`, depending on the regex flavor. In GNU sed, `-r` or `--regexp-extended` uses extended regexes and reduces the amount of escaping needed.

In basic regular expressions, the special characters are:

* `*`
* `^`
* `$`
* `.`
* `[`
* `\`

If you want literal matching and don’t want to worry about regex metacharacters, use `grep -F` or `fgrep`, which matches fixed strings.

Use a shell trap to kill the tmux session when the terminal shell exits. Add this to your interactive shell config:

alias tmuxn='tmux new-session -s $$'
_trap_exit() { tmux kill-session -t $$; }
trap _trap_exit EXIT

Then start tmux with `tmuxn`. The session is named after your shell PID, and when that shell closes, the matching tmux session is killed.

This doesn’t directly change tmux window scaling, but it is the supported guidance in the provided solution for cleaning up the tmux session on terminal close.

There does not seem to be a way to make tmux automatically resize vertical panes to match the visible line length. The closest supported option mentioned is to turn on mouse resizing:

`mouse-resize-pane [on | off]`

With that enabled, tmux captures the mouse and lets you resize panes by dragging their borders.

The evidence says there were two Linux “reverse firewall” apps with GUI-style process-level monitoring and allow/deny control: TuxGuardian and LeopardFlower. However, both are no longer maintained.

It does not provide a current recommended application. The closest guidance it supports is that there is no answer on record, and the question shifts toward building a similar tool from existing Linux tools and libraries, either with a GUI or text-based interface.

For a Linux-based home firewall, IPCop is the one specifically recommended here. It’s described as designed for that purpose and having a long history. Zentyal and SmoothWall were also mentioned as options to look at. If you’re okay with something not based on Linux, pfSense was mentioned too, but it is FreeBSD-based, not Linux.

The only KDE-based distribution mentioned is Chakra, and the response says it has “a very nice installer.” It does not explicitly say it is the best KDE-based distribution. Based on the evidence, Chakra is the closest match if you want a KDE-based distro.

There isn’t a single “best” KDE-based distribution in the thread. The strongest recommendations for a good KDE experience are OpenSuSE Tumbleweed, Chakra, Aptosid, PCLinuxOS, Yoper, and Sabayon. OpenSuSE Tumbleweed is highlighted as a rolling KDE option, and Chakra is noted for a customizable, modular KDE. For a novice-friendly, “just work” KDE setup, the answer especially favors the GUI-centric rolling distros like OpenSuSE Tumbleweed and Chakra.

Set:

XMODIFIERS="@im=none"

This lets X11 handle dead keys, and it works for GTK apps. The evidence says this solution did not work for Qt apps, only GTK.

If you use an input module at the X11 level, X11 no longer handles dead keys or compose keys; the input module does it instead. To use the system Compose database in GTK apps, you’d need a way to switch between XMODIFIERS="@im=ibus" and XMODIFIERS="@im=none", so X11 can handle compose itself. The closest guidance here is that GTK/GNOME may have a configuration or input-method switch for this, but none is confirmed in the provided text.

No application is being “blamed” here. The behavior is about the filesystem and shell, not a specific app.

When a directory is deleted and later recreated, it may get a different inode. Your shell can still be sitting in the old, now-deleted directory entry, so `./run` fails until you `cd` away and back into the recreated directory.

So the closest answer is: the filesystem is recreating the directory as a new object, and the shell’s current working directory becomes stale.

Firefox is the application doing it here. It follows the XDG desktop directory setting, so if `XDG_DESKTOP_DIR` points to `Desktop`, Firefox’s file dialog may auto-create that folder. Changing `~/.config/user-dirs.dirs` to set `XDG_DESKTOP_DIR="$HOME/"` (or another path you want) is the supported fix.

Use `blockdev --getsz /dev/sdx` to get the disk size in 512-byte sectors, then `dd` to write zeros to the last 1MB. Example:

`dd bs=512 if=/dev/zero of=/dev/sdx count=2048 seek=$(( $(blockdev --getsz /dev/sdx) - 2048 ))`

This zeros the final 2048 sectors, which is 1MB.

If you mean the RAID member partitions from a WD MyBook Live disk, the shown layout already marks partitions 1 and 2 as `raid`, while partition 4 is the large `ext4` data partition. The issue described is that the `ext4` filesystem uses a 65536 block size, which standard x86 Linux kernels can’t mount directly. The suggested workaround is to use `fuse-ext2` read-only:

`fuseext2 -o ro -o sync_read /dev/sdb4 /mnt/`

If you’re trying to find the “position” of the RAID drives, the evidence doesn’t give a direct command for that; it only shows the partition table and how to access the big partition.

For software RAID, `cat /proc/mdstat` shows whether any md devices exist, and `mdadm -D /dev/mdxx` gives RAID level, chunk size, and other details.

For hardware RAID, `cat /proc/mdstat` may show nothing. Check whether a RAID controller is present with:

`lspci -vv | grep -i raid`

If it is hardware RAID, the RAID level and configuration usually require the vendor’s management tool, for example:

`omreport storage vdisk` for Dell  
`arcconf getconfig 2` for Adaptec

So the closest answer is: use `mdadm -D` for software RAID, and `lspci` plus the vendor tool for hardware RAID.

If you want apt-get to stop trying to pull in optional packages, install with:

apt-get --no-install-recommends install foo

If the issue is unmet dependencies that you don’t actually want installed, the supported workaround here is to create a dummy package with equivs to satisfy apt’s dependency check. Edit the control file’s Package field, build it, then install the generated .deb with dpkg.

The only supported guidance here is to avoid installing Python from source on top of the distro-managed Python environment. If you need a different Python version, use a VM, virtualenv, or install the distro package instead of replacing system Python. This helps keep apt’s dependency tracking intact.

If your goal is to stop apt from removing something it thinks is unused, the evidence doesn’t give a specific apt-mark or auto-remove command. It only says not to interfere with the distro’s Python packages and to use an isolated environment or the distro’s repository version.

Mark the package as manually installed so autoremove won’t treat it as automatically installed and eligible for removal:

apt-mark manual python-socksipy

The best fix is to build your package with the correct dependencies, but this command is the quick way to prevent apt-get from autoremoving it.

What you’re seeing is consistent with the program’s stdout being buffered when it is not connected to a terminal. In that case, output may be held until the program exits, so SSH displays both lines together.

The provided material does not give a specific fix, but the usual direction is to make the remote program flush its output explicitly or run it with unbuffered/line-buffered I/O if that option exists. For example, printing and then flushing after each line would make “foo” appear before the sleep ends.

It’s not line buffering. The program is leaving the terminal in an underline/formatting state by emitting terminal control codes and not resetting them afterward.

Try running:
echo -e '\e[0m'
or just:
reset

That should restore normal display.

If a program does this, it should be fixed by the software author; it’s not a Linux or SSH issue.

If you mean SSH sessions, the closest supported solution here is GNU screen. It keeps a scrollback buffer of recent output and lets you disconnect and reconnect later, which fits the “drop in, look, drop out” use case.

This does not describe SSH itself being line buffered; rather, it suggests using screen to capture and view the session output.

If you need more than a screenful or two of history, this answer doesn’t cover that.

Stop using the filesystem right away. If you can, stop the VM or remount the affected volume read-only:

mount -o remount,ro /home/

If it’s ext3/ext4, the data may still be there, but the directory pointers are gone. Recovery is possible, but not guaranteed, and it’s harder for text and uncommon file types. Tools mentioned include photorec, foremost, unrm, and ext3undel.

If you only deleted `/home/pi`, the same general advice applies: stop writes immediately and try recovery tools.

If the directories were only renamed or moved, not actually deleted, you can usually reverse the move/rename.

The suggested reversal is:

for f in *
do echo mv -v "$f" "${f%"#_*"}"
done

Keep the echo first to verify it will rename things correctly before running it for real.

If your `/home/pi` items were moved somewhere else, like another directory, this should help move them back. If they were truly deleted, this does not cover recovery from deletion.

Use multitail. It extends tail -f and can highlight log lines by content, including colors you configure.

Example:
multitail -c /path/to/log

Or define rules such as:
cs_re:green:INFO
cs_re:red:SEVERE

If you can’t install extra tools, a fallback is:
tail -f /path/to/log | awk '
  /INFO/ {print "\033[32m" $0 "\033[39m"}
  /SEVERE/ {print "\033[31m" $0 "\033[39m"}
'

Using `tail -f` on a large file should not be a problem by itself: the behavior described is that it skips to the end with `lseek`, so the file size should not matter much. That suggests your 1 GB log is fine for near real-time monitoring.

What this does not cover is Solaris 10 specifics, rollover handling, or whether `grep` adds any meaningful overhead in your exact setup. The closest guidance supported here is to test `tail -f` on your system to confirm it behaves similarly, since that is what determines the performance.

On Linux/AIX, the evidence does not show a built-in way to “pretty tail” multiple files with a single tail command using `-f`/`-0f`. It says `tail` can only process one file at a time in Linux for that form, and AIX rejects `-0f` as invalid.

The supported workaround is to run separate tails in the background:

tail -f file1 &
tail -f file2 &

If you want each output labeled, pipe each through `sed`:

tail -f file1 | sed 's/^/file1: /' &
tail -f file2 | sed 's/^/file2: /' &

For following many files by pattern, the evidence suggests using a custom script.

If you’re trying to act on a range of lines, the closest supported guidance here is to use a line range with `:s`. For example, `:'x,.s/$/    /` adds 4 spaces to the end of each line from mark `x` to the current line.

For a visual selection, `:'<,'>s/$/    /` does the same.

This evidence does not show how to search for a pattern and include the 4 lines before each match.

grep prints whole lines, where a line is delimited by a newline character, not by what wraps on your screen.

To show lines matching a pattern and the 4 lines before each, use:

grep -B 4 'pattern' filename

If you want line numbers too:

grep -n -B 4 'pattern' filename

Use the clipboard selection, not the default primary selection:

uptime | xclip -selection c

or equivalently:

uptime | xclip -selection clipboard

The evidence says the default xclip output goes to the primary selection, which pastes with the middle mouse button. To paste into applications like gedit or Firefox using the normal Paste action, copy to the clipboard selection with `-selection c` / `-selection clipboard`.

The provided solution is for splitting a file into chunks and piping each chunk to a command; it does not cover bulk converting line endings across a directory tree.

For line-break conversion, the closest guidance it supports is that you’d need to process the files in a script rather than with a built-in “split to stdout” feature. To convert files in a branch, you’d typically iterate over each file and rewrite it with the desired line endings using a tool or script that reads and writes the file contents.
Use dos2unix and unix2dos. Wrap them in a shell script that matches all your source files, and run it over the branch to convert CRLF to LF or vice versa.

Use find, not ls. The idea is to list directories with their modification times, sort them numerically, and take the oldest one.

For example:

IFS= read -r -d $'\0' line < <(
  find . -maxdepth 1 -type d -printf '%T@ %p\0' 2>/dev/null | sort -z -n
)
file="${line#* }"

This finds directories in the current folder only, prints each directory’s mtime as “seconds since 1970” plus its path, separates entries with NUL characters, sorts by time, then reads the first (oldest) result into line. The file variable strips off the timestamp, leaving the path.

If you want, I can also show how to adapt this to delete the oldest directory or move the oldest file.

You can sort the matching files by the embedded date string, then move them one by one:

for i in $(grep dateishere *.html | sed 's/\(.*\):.* \([0-9]*dateishere\).*/\1 \2/' | sort -k 2 | awk '{print $1}')
do
  mv "$i" /other/location/
done

This moves the oldest date first, assuming the date is in the `XXXXXXXXdateishere` format and sorts correctly as a string.

The drive is mounted read-only (`type vfat (ro, ...)`), so regular users can’t write to it until it’s mounted read/write.

The answer given suggests:
- create a mount point, e.g. `/media/myUsb`
- remount the partition with read/write permissions:
  `sudo mount -o remount,rw /dev/sdc1 /media/myUsb`

It also says the issue may be mounting under `/run`. This only covers remounting the drive as `rw`; it does not explain how to make that persist automatically or how to set permissions beyond the mount options shown.

For a native filesystem like ext4, the mounted drive’s files keep their normal Unix ownership and permissions. To let regular users write, make sure the files and directories on the drive are owned by the same user/group IDs on the machines that will mount it, or as root change permissions after mounting with chmod -R a+rwX /mountpoint/of/device. If you keep creating files, use permissions like 666 for files and 777 for directories. For non-native filesystems like vfat or ntfs, mount options can set the owner and permissions.

With the drive unmounted, remove access to the mount point:

`sudo chmod a-rwx /mnt/external`

A mounted filesystem does not use the permissions of the mount-point directory; it uses the permissions from the root of the mounted filesystem. When nothing is mounted there, the directory permissions on the underlying filesystem apply.

So for regular users, set the permissions on the external drive’s filesystem itself, and keep the mount point inaccessible when unmounted.

A filename can contain newlines; that’s one of the reasons newline-separated `ls` output is unsafe to parse. The guidance here is not to rely on `ls` for machine-readable filename lists. If you need to handle arbitrary filenames, use a tool or language that can process them directly, or keep the path values as data rather than parsing printed text. The cited answer also suggests that if this starts feeling too complex for a shell script, rewriting in a better scripting language is the safer path.

Use ANSI-C quoting, not `"\n"` inside double quotes.

For example:

`find . -name $'*\n*'`

Or, equivalently, concatenate quoted pieces:

`find . -name '*'$'\n''*'`

These patterns match filenames containing a literal newline.

Use a hard link when you want another directory entry to the same file data and inode, and you want it to keep working even if the original name is moved or deleted. Hard links only work within the same filesystem, and they can’t be made to directories.

Use a symbolic (soft) link when you want a link to a path instead of the file itself. Symlinks can cross filesystems, can point to directories, and are useful when you want the link to follow a filename/location rather than a specific inode. They break if the target is moved or deleted.

Hard links for directories are not allowed. If you need something that survives renaming the visible directory name, one approach is to keep the real directory in a hidden location and make your other directories symbolic links to it. Then you can rename the visible links without breaking them.

A suggested pattern is to create the real directory under something like a hidden folder and symlink to it. The provided example creates a unique real directory and then links a chosen name to it.

Hardlinks were also mentioned as useful for file management tools, but the evidence only covers directory hard links being disallowed and symlinks as the workaround.

Use a hard link when you want another directory entry for the same file with no extra size or speed penalty. A hard link is built into the filesystem, so opening it doesn’t require following a separate link, and it doesn’t use disk space for link text.

Use a soft link when you want a link that can point to something like a pathname and is more flexible, but it does add a little indirection and small disk space overhead.

A concrete example from the evidence: .. is a real hard link in Unix filesystems, tying directories together.

Hard links are additional directory entries for the same file data (inode). They’re useful when you want the file to remain accessible even if one name is moved or deleted, but they only work within the same filesystem and for files, not directories.

Soft links (symbolic links) store a path to another file or directory. They’re useful when you want a shortcut to something that may be on a different filesystem or when you need to link to a directory. They can break if the target is moved or deleted.

A hard link is a second name for the same file data, so the file stays accessible even if one name is removed. A soft link (symlink) is a pointer to a path, so it can break if the target is renamed or moved.

For directories, hard links are not allowed. A suggested workaround is to keep the real directory in a fixed hidden location and make both visible directories soft links to it, so renaming the visible names does not break the link.

A hard link is a second directory entry to the same file data, built into the filesystem. It has no extra indirection, so there’s no size or speed penalty like a soft link, and it continues to work even if the original filename is removed. Hard links are what tie Unix directories together; for example, `..` is a real hard link back to the parent directory.

A soft link is a separate file that points to another path. It adds a small amount of space and lookup time because the kernel must dereference it when opening the target. Soft links are useful when you want a shortcut to a path, especially across filesystems, but they can break if the target is deleted or moved.

The evidence only mentions changing the log-in screen sound in Linux Mint 11, not the background. So it does not confirm whether the log-in screen background can be changed. The closest supported guidance is that Linux Mint 11 login-screen-related settings may be adjustable through Control Center → Startup Applications Preferences, but only for the GNOME Login Sound based on the provided text.

If the MySQL directory was deleted, the best-supported recovery approach is to keep the system powered off and boot from a rescue disk such as SystemRescueCD. Use file recovery tools there, especially PhotoRec and TestDisk. Another tool worth trying is extundelete, though it may need to be installed separately or added to the rescue media. This is the closest guidance available for recovering /var/lib/mysql after deletion or reinstall.

To restore the MySQL directory by reinstalling, remove the MySQL packages and delete the data/config directories, then reinstall:

apt-get purge mysql-server mysql-common mysql-client-<version>
rm -rf /var/lib/mysql
rm -rf /etc/mysql*

After that, reinstall MySQL. This is the closest supported approach for recreating the MySQL directory/files. If your goal is only to recover deleted data, this does not cover data restoration.

If you accidentally changed ownership under /var and MySQL won’t start, the part covered here says /var/lib/mysql is not managed by rpm. Its files are normally owned by mysql:mysql, so restoring that ownership should fix it:

chown -R mysql:mysql /var/lib/mysql

If other files under /var were affected and they belong to RPM-managed packages, rpm --setperms --setguids can reset those package permissions.

The evidence only shows that the asterisk is used in forms like UN*X or *nix to indicate that some letters are skipped or replaced, but it doesn’t give the full reason for why that convention became associated with Unix. The closest supported guidance is that the asterisk is a wildcard-style stand-in, so UN*X can mean Unix-like names or variants without spelling every letter out. It does not confirm a specific historical explanation.

The “*” is used because “Unix” often stands for a wider family of Unix-like systems, not just one exact operating system. In the evidence, the big reason the transition is slow is that customers face a lot of cost and risk moving between UNIX vendors or from UNIX to Linux: software compatibility, porting custom apps, retraining staff, and long testing/migration timelines. So when people mention Unix online, they may mean the broader *NIX world, where many systems are related but still different enough to matter.

A shell is a command-line program that accepts commands and runs them.

An xshell is a terminal emulator: a graphical program that displays a terminal window and lets you run shell programs inside it.

So the main difference is:
- Shells: the command processor itself
- XShells: the graphical window used to run a shell

In practice, choosing a Shells menu entry starts that shell in your default terminal emulator, while choosing an XShells entry starts your default shell in the selected terminal emulator.

The main difference described is that vim has many more features than plain vi. Notable ones mentioned are multiple windows/tabs, visual highlighting, online help, macro recording, multiple undo/redo, command/search history, more powerful pattern matching, word completion, a built-in file navigator, and commands that operate on all buffers/args/windows.

If you think you’re using vi on many Linux systems, you may actually be using vim, since vi is often mapped to vim. If :help works, multiple undos work, or :version works, that indicates vim, not vi.

If you meant “different shells” like bash, zsh, and sh, this source doesn’t cover that.

From the provided material, the only concrete difference mentioned is for zsh: it has autocompletion support, a right-side prompt, and multiline command editing. The question also names bash, csh, Korn, and zsh as popular shells, but no specific differences for those others are given here.

So, the evidence supports saying shells can differ in user-interface and editing features, with zsh highlighted for those conveniences. It does not provide a broader comparison of significant differences among shells.

To check the distro version and kernel version, use:

cat /etc/gentoo-release
uname -r

For example, these might return something like:
Gentoo Base System release 2.1
3.1.6-gentoo

If you want package-based Gentoo info, you can also use:
equery list baselayout
eselect kernel list

Those commands show the installed Gentoo base system and available kernel symlinks.

A file descriptor number is not the direct index into the kernel’s open file table. It is an index into a process-specific file descriptor table. That table entry then points to an entry in the kernel’s global open file table, and also stores file-descriptor flags.

So two different processes can both have fd 4, but fd 4 in each process may point to different open-file-table entries. Also, different descriptors can point to the same file if their table entries reference the same open-file-table entry.

From an SSH session, it’s not practical to “log into” an existing GNOME/Xorg session or bring up the whole desktop on Windows via PuTTY alone. The suggested alternatives are VNC, XDMCP, or FreeNX.

If you only need to start apps remotely, you can SSH in and launch them on the machine’s local X session, but controlling the full desktop/session is better handled with VNC or FreeNX, possibly over an SSH tunnel. If you really want to display the remote login/desktop on Windows, you’d need a local X server on Windows and a way to start the remote display manager there, which is the hard path.

The provided information does not include an answer for remotely controlling an Xorg session. It only shows a related question about creating a customized X session in RHEL 6 to run a single application without a desktop, and that no answer was recorded.

Closest guidance supported by this is that X sessions can be customized to start just one application instead of a full desktop. If your goal is remote control, you would need additional documentation or a separate solution not covered here.

XDG_SESSION_COOKIE is not for remote X control itself. It was used by ConsoleKit as a session “secret” stored in the environment, and later session management moved to systemd-logind. It is not related to DISPLAY.

For ssh remote login to control a local X session, the key point is authentication to connect to the X server, not XDG_SESSION_COOKIE. DISPLAY identifies which X server/display to talk to, while the cookie/session mechanism is about permission to connect.

So: no, XDG_SESSION_COOKIE is not the thing that enables remote control of the local Xorg session; it’s about session authentication/management.

The provided material doesn’t explain how to access the X display from a cron job when using gdm3.

What it does support is that if you want to start a GDM/GNOME X session inside an existing X11 session, you can use xnest or xephyr to run an X session in a window. That would let you switch to it with Alt+Tab, but it is not a cron-specific display-access solution.

With gdm3, the X session usually starts with xauth cookie setup, not just by launching X directly. The closest guidance from the thread is to do similar xauth setup before starting the X server, like the xserverrc script does:

xauth -f $auth source - <<-EOF
add $tcpip $cookie
add $unix  $cookie
add ${host}/unix$dspnum $cookie
EOF

So for a cron job, you’d need to use the same display authorization method for the active X display, rather than relying on plain `DISPLAY=:0` alone. The thread does not show a gdm3-specific cron example, but it indicates xauth cookie handling is the key step.

Cron jobs are user-specific unless you create a system-level cron entry, which runs once at the scheduled time as a chosen user. So you do not need one run per logged-in user unless you explicitly duplicate the job. For accessing an X display from cron under gdm3, the usual approach is to run the job as the graphical user and set the correct display-related environment for that session. The evidence here does not provide the exact gdm3/X11 variables or commands, only that a single cron job runs once per schedule and that jobs can be user-specific or system-level.

The thread says the issue was with XQuartz 2.7.5 on the Mac; downgrading to XQuartz 2.7.4 made the old Xephyr/ssh X11 forwarding commands work again. It doesn’t specifically mention xrandr, but if your xrandr call is happening over the same X11-forwarded setup, the closest supported guidance is to try XQuartz 2.7.4 instead of 2.7.5.

The behavior described was ultimately traced to a hardware defect in the display itself. It happened even when connected to different computers, including a Windows 7 machine, and buying a new display resolved it. This doesn’t provide a software fix for using xrandr over SSH, but it does suggest that if you’re seeing display detection problems, the monitor/cable/adapter hardware may be the cause.

That Xlib warning is harmless and can be ignored. It means the libraries support an extension that the X server does not support yet, so it is not necessarily an error. The suggested fix in the thread is not to install anything; no package change helped there.

X11 is the communication protocol between an X client and an X server. Xlib is a library clients use to talk to the X server using that protocol.

So if you see “Xlib: No protocol specified,” it means Xlib tried to connect to the X server but wasn’t allowed to. The evidence doesn’t explain the exact cause of that error, only the relationship between X11, X server, and Xlib.

X server is not just a single library; it’s a server process. You don’t access it directly because clients normally communicate with it through Xlib or another client library.

The issue is with `DISPLAY`. The suggested fix is to use the IP address of the Windows machine, not its computer name:

`setenv DISPLAY IPAddress:0`

The thread also indicates you should open the program in another terminal window on windows-solaris. This directly addresses the “Can’t open display” / “No protocol specified” error in the example.

Cron usually won’t have your desktop DBUS session, so `notify-send` can run but never reach the GUI. The fix is to set `DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS` in the cron script.

One way is to save it when you log in:

```sh
touch $HOME/.dbus/Xdbus
chmod 600 $HOME/.dbus/Xdbus
env | grep DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS > $HOME/.dbus/Xdbus
echo 'export DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS' >> $HOME/.dbus/Xdbus
```

Then source it from the cron script before calling `notify-send`:

```sh
if [ -r "$HOME/.dbus/Xdbus" ]; then
  . "$HOME/.dbus/Xdbus"
fi
```

This covers the missing piece beyond `DISPLAY` and `XAUTHORITY`.

A cron/anacron job can’t open a GUI display directly, so Zenity/KDialog from the cron task will fail with “cannot open display.” The working pattern here is to decouple the notification from the cron job:

1. Have the root cron script write a message to a per-user file, e.g. `/home/$USERN/.updateNotification.txt`.
2. Run a small script in the user’s session/autostart that periodically checks for that file.

Then bring your interfaces down:

`ip link set <interface> down`

After that, enable and start NetworkManager:

`systemctl enable NetworkManager`
`systemctl start NetworkManager`

If you want the GNOME applet too, install:

`pacman -Syu networkmanager network-manager-applet`

You can’t completely disable swap for a cgroup by setting swappiness to 0. That only lowers the tendency to swap; it does not guarantee pages won’t be swapped under memory pressure.

If you need pages to never be swapped, the supported approach is to lock them in memory with mlock(). cgroups swappiness cannot fully prevent swapping.

For cgroups specifically, swappiness also can’t be changed for:
- the root cgroup
- a cgroup with sub-cgroups below it
- a non-root cgroup in a hierarchy

So the closest supported guidance is: use swappiness to reduce swapping, and use mlock() to keep critical pages resident.

To completely disable swap, turn it off with:

sudo swapoff -a

This disables all active swap. If you want to re-enable it later, use:

sudo swapon -a

Be careful: if you don’t have enough RAM, turning off swap can cause out-of-memory errors and may lead the kernel to kill processes to free memory.

For accounts, the supported way to disable logins completely is:

usermod --lock --expiredate 1970-01-02 <username>

`--lock` alone only blocks password logins; key-based logins can still work. `--expiredate` disables the account, and any date before today can be used. To re-enable later:

usermod --unlock --expiredate '' <username>

awk '{a=gensub(/.*#([0-9]+)(\").*/,"\\1","g",$0); if(a~/[0-9]+/) gsub(/[0-9]+\"/, a+11"\"", $0); print $0}'

This extracts the number after #, adds 11 to it, then replaces the matching number before the quote.

This outputs `123`.

So the supported guidance here is to use a regex that extracts the quoted content, rather than relying on `{0,3}` in AWK.

```bash
if [ yes != "$STDBUF" ]; then

fi
```

Use a named pipe. It’s a file node on disk, but the data passing through it stays in memory, not on disk.

Example:

mkfifo fifo
echo -e "hello world\nnext line\nline 3" > fifo

This will block until something reads from the pipe. In another shell:

cat fifo

Then the writer unblocks. You can also background the writer with &.

The pipe has a 64k buffer on Linux and will block the writer when full, so data won’t be lost unless the writer is killed too early.

`${i%.avi}.mp4` is Bash parameter expansion. It takes the value of `i`, removes the shortest matching suffix `.avi` from the end if present, then adds `.mp4`.

Example:
- `i="video.avi"` → `video.mp4`
- `i="clip.avi.backup"` → unchanged by `.avi` removal, then `.mp4` is appended

It’s often used to rename or convert filenames by changing the extension.

In sh-like shells, `${x%% *}` is not a job reference. It is parameter expansion that removes the longest matching suffix from the value of `x`. The pattern here is ` *` (a space followed by anything), so it strips everything from the first space onward, leaving only the part before the first space.

Example:
- `x="hello world test"`
- `${x%% *}` → `hello`

So it’s commonly used to get the first word from a variable.

`${x%% *}` is shell parameter expansion that removes the longest match of ` *` from the end of `x`.

In practice, it strips everything from the last space onward, leaving the part before the last space.

Example:
- `x="hello world again"`
- `${x%% *}` → `hello`

If there’s no space in `x`, it stays unchanged.

`${x%% *}` is shell parameter expansion, not a regular expression.

It means: take the value of `x` and remove the longest match of the pattern `*` preceded by a space, from the end of the string. In practice, it strips everything from the first space onward, leaving the part before the first space.

Example:
`x="hello world test"`
`${x%% *}` → `hello`

This is the same kind of expansion as `${0##*/}` and `${0%/*}`, just using `%`/`%%` to remove from the end instead of `#`/`##` from the beginning.

`${foo##*.}` is parameter expansion, not filename globbing. `##` means “remove the longest matching prefix” from `$foo`. The pattern `*.` matches everything up to and including the last dot, so for `report.tar.gz` it removes `report.tar.` and leaves `gz`.

Examples:
- `foo=notes.txt` → `${foo##*.}` = `txt`
- `foo=/path/a.b/c.tar.gz` → `${foo##*.}` = `gz`

It works best when the string contains a dot. If there’s no dot, the whole value is returned unchanged.

`${foo##*.}` is shell parameter expansion that removes the longest matching prefix ending in a dot, leaving what comes after the last `.` in `foo`. So if `foo` is `archive.tar.gz`, `${foo##*.}` becomes `gz`.

This only works as expected when `foo` contains a dot. If there’s no dot, the value stays unchanged.

`${foo##*.}` is not brace expansion; it’s shell parameter expansion.

`##` removes the longest match of the pattern `*.` from the left side of the value in `foo`. Since `*.` means “everything up to and including the last dot,” what remains is the file extension.

Examples:
- `file.txt` → `txt`
- `archive.tar.gz` → `gz`
- `noextension` → unchanged, because there’s no `.` to match

So it works by taking the variable’s value and stripping the longest prefix ending in a dot.

#!/bin/busybox sh
sed="busybox sed"

search_in() {
    searchterm="$1"
    searchdir="$2"
    prefix="$3"
    (
        cd "$searchdir"
        for file in *
        do
            if [ -d "$file" ]; then
                search_in "$searchterm" "$file" "$prefix\\/$file"
            else
                $sed -rn '/'"$searchterm"'/s/(.*)/'"$prefix\\/$file"': \1/gp' "$file"
            fi
        done
    )
}

This happens because the user’s home directory is encrypted and mounted only after a physical login. SSH public-key auth needs sshd to read `authorized_keys` before login, but that file is inside the unmounted home directory, so authentication fails.

The workaround is to move `authorized_keys` outside the encrypted home and point sshd to it, for example:

`AuthorizedKeysFile .ssh/authorized_keys /home/%u-authorized_keys`

Then restart sshd.

This still won’t mount the home directory for SSH; if home decryption depends on a password, SSH key login won’t provide it.

For SSH, stderr and stdout are separate. In the example, `2>&1` is being applied on the remote side only to the last command, so only that command’s stderr is merged.

Use one of these patterns:

```sh

for i in 10.38.227.229 10.38.164.103
do

done >> log 2>&1
```

Or merge on the remote side for all commands:

```sh
ssh "auto21@$i" "{ $command; } 2>&1"
```

Or:

```sh
ssh "auto21@$i" "exec 2>&1; $command"
```

This should let you collect output and errors for each IP in the local log.

You can do this by looping over the .xml files, checking that the matching .mxf file exists, and only moving both when each is at least 5 minutes old.

One issue in the sample script is a typo: it checks $no_ext, but it should check $mxf.

A corrected version is:

#!/usr/bin/env bash

SOURCEDIR="/dir/to/source"
DESTDIR="/destination/dir"

for f in "$SOURCEDIR"/*.xml; do
    [ -f "$f" ] || continue
    [ "$(( $(date +%s) - $(stat -c %Y "$f") ))" -ge 300 ] || continue

    mxf="$SOURCEDIR/$(basename "$f" .xml).mxf"
    [ -f "$mxf" ] || continue
    [ "$(( $(date +%s) - $(stat -c %Y "$mxf") ))" -ge 300 ] || continue

    mv -v "$f" "$mxf" "$DESTDIR"
done

Load average is basically the average length of the run queue: how many processes or threads are ready to run and waiting for CPU time. So on a modern multicore CPU, it’s not limited to 1; several CPU-consuming tasks can raise it well above 1. A multithreaded process can also contribute more than 1 if multiple threads are runnable. A load average below the number of CPU cores generally means the machine has enough CPU capacity; above that, some runnable tasks are waiting in queue.

Load average is not “CPU usage over the last 1/5/15 minutes.” It’s a measure of how many tasks were runnable or stuck waiting, so it can be high even when current CPU use is low. That’s why a later `top`/`htop` view won’t show what caused an earlier spike.

For modern CPUs, the same idea still applies: more cores can handle more runnable tasks, so a load of 4 means something different on a 4-core system than on a 16-core system. The evidence here specifically supports using `atop`, which records snapshots over time so you can look back and see what was running during earlier load spikes.

$var and "$var" are not the same in use.

$var expands to the variable’s contents, but if you use it unquoted, the result can be split on spaces and treated as glob patterns. So a value like spaced filename becomes two arguments, and * can expand to matching files.

"$var" treats the value as one atomic string, preserving spaces and preventing glob expansion. That’s why it’s usually the safer form, especially with commands like rm.

The curly braces in ${var} are optional for a simple variable name in POSIX shell; they’re mainly useful for more complex parameter expansions.

`"$var"` and `"${var}"` both expand the variable inside double quotes, so in many cases they behave the same.

The difference is that `${var}` is the more explicit form and is useful when the variable name is next to other text, so the shell knows exactly where the variable name ends. For example, `"${var}1"` means the value of `var` followed by `1`, while `"$var1"` refers to a different variable named `var1`.

There’s no difference in simple cases: `$var` is a shortened form of `${var}`.

`"${var}"` is better when you want to quote the value so spaces or glob characters don’t get split or expanded. Example: `rm -- "$var"`.

`${var}` also allows extra parameter expansion features that `$var` can’t, such as substring removal or array-style references, though some of those aren’t portable.

For plain variable expansion in POSIX shells, the braces are optional.

Because SSH is still allowed to try password-based methods after public key authentication fails or isn’t available. To stop it from prompting, disable password authentication on the client side:

A likely cause is incorrect ownership or permissions on the remote account’s ~/.ssh directory or home directory. The directory should be owned by you, ~/.ssh should be 0700, and your home directory should not be writable by group/others. If those permissions are wrong, ssh may ignore authorized_keys and fall back to asking for a password.

A common reason is that sshd rejects the key because permissions are too open on your home directory, .ssh directory, or authorized_keys file. The suggested fix is to make $HOME and $HOME/.ssh more restrictive for group and other, and ensure authorized_keys also has tight permissions. Once sshd can trust those paths, public key login should work without falling back to a password prompt.

If SSH key login works for root but not for a normal user, the usual fix is to make sure the user’s home directory, `.ssh` directory, and `authorized_keys` all belong to that user and are not writable by others:

`chown Testuser ~Testuser ~Testuser/.ssh ~Testuser/.ssh/authorized_keys`
`chmod go-w ~Testuser ~Testuser/.ssh ~Testuser/.ssh/authorized_keys`

Also ensure `authorized_keys` is readable by the user. Using `ssh-copy-id` is the preferred way because it sets permissions correctly.

SSH is only trying the default private key filenames: ~/.ssh/identity, ~/.ssh/id_rsa, ~/.ssh/id_dsa, ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa, and ~/.ssh/id_ed25519. If your key is named something else, it won’t be used automatically.

To fix it, either:
- specify it with ssh -i /path/to/key
- add it in your client config with IdentityFile
- load it into your ssh agent with ssh-add

Also, it’s the private key that SSH reads for authentication, not the public key file.

This fits an encrypted home directory or pam_mount setup. Public-key SSH does not send a password, so pam_mount can’t use it to mount the home directory. Also, sshd must read authorized_keys before login, so if that file is inside the encrypted/mounted home, authentication fails until you do a physical login that mounts it.

A workaround is to move authorized_keys out of the home directory and point sshd to it, for example:

AuthorizedKeysFile .ssh/authorized_keys /home/%u-authorized_keys

Then restart sshd.

This will fix key lookup, but it won’t decrypt or mount the home directory for SSH sessions.

`grep`/`egrep` work per line, so they won’t match across multiple lines. For multiple-line matching, one supported approach is `sed`, for example:

Replace `foo` with the starting pattern, `bar` with the ending pattern, and `your_regex` with the full multi-line regex you want to match. `-n` suppresses automatic printing, `N` appends the next line, and `p` prints only when the full pattern matches.

- sed:

- perl:
  perl -ne 'print if /pattern1/ && /pattern2/'

grep 'pattern1\|pattern2'

if &term =~ "screen"

elseif &term =~ "xterm"

endif

map  <F13> <C-CR>
map! <F13> <C-CR>

Use `history 1` in `PROMPT_COMMAND` to get the just-executed command line.

For example:

```bash
prompt_function () {
  local prompt_history="$(history 1)"
  prompt_history=${prompt_history:7}
  echo -En $'\033[38;5;2m'"$prompt_history"$'\033[0m\n'
}
PROMPT_COMMAND=prompt_function
```

This reprints the last command before the next prompt. The simpler version is:

```bash
PROMPT_COMMAND='echo -en "\033[38;5;2m"; history 1; echo -en "\033[0m\n"'
```

If you want to remove duplicate `$PATH` entries, an awk approach is to print each item only once:

awk -v RS=: -v ORS=: '!seen[$0]++' <<< "$PATH"

If you want normal newline-separated output instead of colon-separated, you can do:

awk -v RS=: '!seen[$0]++' <<< "$PATH"

This keeps the first occurrence of each path and removes repeats.

If you need to compare two files/sets of entries, the provided example only shows how to filter unique lines, not a full `$PATH`-specific script.

Use awk to keep only the first occurrence of each PATH entry, treating each entry as the key:

awk -F: '!seen[$1]++'

This is the same idea as using awk to remove duplicate CSV rows by a chosen column. For a PATH-like colon-separated list, $1 would be the first entry. If you need to deduplicate an existing PATH variable rather than a file, you’d need to apply the same pattern to the colon-separated items after splitting them.

Use:

awk '!NF || !seen[$0]++'

This keeps every empty line (`!NF`) and removes duplicate non-empty lines by remembering each line in `seen`. An equivalent form is:

awk '!(NF && seen[$0]++)'

If you want to apply the same idea to `$PATH`, split it on `:` and use the same duplicate-tracking logic for each element.

Set the setgid bit on the directory so new items inherit its group:

setfacl -d -m o::rx /path/to/directory

You can verify with:

getfacl /path/to/directory

This makes items created under it keep the directory’s group and default permissions.

By default, GNU sort uses your locale’s collation order, not a universal fixed order. In many locales, that means digits first, then lowercase and uppercase grouped by letter, with lowercase before uppercase. In the example shown, default sort gives:

1 2 3 a A b B c C

If you set LC_COLLATE=C, you get uppercase before lowercase:

1 2 3 A B C a b c

So the default depends on locale. If you want a different case order, you’d need a custom locale.

For `ls`, the evidence says the sort order depends on options: `-t` sorts by file modification time, `-S` sorts by size, and `-r` reverses the order. For exact default behavior, check `man ls`.

The default sort order in Linux here is locale-dependent, not “underscore first.” In the example, `ls` uses the system’s collation order from `LC_COLLATE` / the current locale, which in `en_US` does not put `_` before letters.

The likely cause is files hidden behind mount points, so `du` on `/` won’t see them even though `df` counts the space.

A good way to check is to bind-mount the root filesystem somewhere else and run `du` there, while excluding mounted filesystems from the search. For example:

`mkdir /root/root-rebound`
`mount -o bind / /root/root-rebound`
`du -sc $(df -P | awk 'NR>2 {print "/root/root-rebound" $6}')`

That lets you inspect the parts of `/` that are normally covered by other mounts.

The space issue is likely being affected by what filesystem/device you’re actually checking, not just the simple total of Used + Available. The supported guidance here is to look at all mounted filesystems with `df -a`, and also run `df` against the specific directory that’s filling up, like `df /var/log`, to see which device backs it. If you need to find where the space is going, checking the largest directories with `du` is the closest next step supported here.

If the live system uses tmpfs for `/`, `/tmp`, and `/run`, then “disk space” there is really RAM-backed space shared with running programs. Filling it with files/logs reduces memory available to Firefox, X, rdesktop, etc., and memory-heavy apps reduce space available to the tmpfs. That can cause disappearing/reappearing files, crashes, lost session history, and other odd behavior. The space is often about half of total RAM by default, so you can run out even with free physical memory seeming available. The closest guidance supported here is to reduce files on the RAM filesystem and watch memory/tmpfs usage together.

A superblock is the filesystem’s top-level control structure; it stores information needed to understand the filesystem layout and find its data.

An inode is the on-disk record for a single file. It traditionally stores the file’s metadata and the block numbers where the file’s contents live. The filename is not in the inode.

A dentry is a directory entry: the mapping from a filename to an inode number. This is why multiple names can point to the same inode (hard links).

A file is the actual named object you access through a directory entry, backed by an inode and its data blocks.

To send the output of one command to another, use a pipe:

`command1 | command2`

If you need to combine several commands first, group them and then pipe the group:

`(command1; command2 | command3; command4) | command5`

or in bash:

`{ command1; command2 | command3; command4; } | command5`

If you need the output as one argument, use command substitution:

`command2 "$(command1)"`

If you need file-like input in bash, use process substitution:

`command <(command2 | grep pattern)`

In Bash, standard input redirection goes after the command name:

`command < file`

If you want the output of one command to become input to another, use a pipeline or process substitution, and attach the redirection to the command that should receive the input:

`command1 | command2`

`grep bar <(echo $'foo\nbar\nbaz')`

If you need multiple commands grouped first, wrap them in a subshell or group, then pipe them:

`(command1; command2 | command3; command4) | command5`

`<` redirects a command’s standard input from a file. `|` sends the standard output of one command into the standard input of the next command.

They are not the same: a pipe creates a subshell, while input redirection from a file does not.

If `sudo` seems not to “pass through” after a redirection operator, the key point is that redirection applies to the command it is attached to, not to the next command in a pipeline.

Because the `while read ...` loop is fed by a pipe, Bash runs that loop in a subshell. Any `FILES+=($snack)` done there changes only the subshell’s copy of the array, and those changes are lost when the loop ends. That’s why only values added outside the piped loop remain.

To keep the array, don’t pipe into the loop. Use process substitution or redirection instead, for example:

`while read snack; do FILES+=($snack); done < <(find /var/candy -name "chocolate_[0-9]")`

or:

`while read snack; do FILES+=($snack); done <<<"$(find /var/candy -name "chocolate_[0-9]")"`

Multithreaded processes can add more than one to the load, and load can exceed the number of CPU cores when some tasks are waiting for free CPU time.

`${foo##*.}` is Bash parameter expansion that removes the longest matching prefix from `foo`.

- `##` = strip the longest matching prefix
- `*.` = any characters ending with a dot

So it deletes everything through the last `.` and leaves what follows. That’s why it can be used to get a file extension:

`file.tar.gz` → `gz`

If there is no dot, it won’t strip anything, so the value stays unchanged.

`${foo##*.}` is Bash parameter expansion that removes the longest matching prefix ending in `*.` from the value of `foo`, leaving what comes after the last dot. So it’s commonly used to get a file extension.

Examples:
- `foo="archive.tar.gz"` → `gz`
- `foo="photo.jpg"` → `jpg`
- `foo="README"` → unchanged, since there’s no dot to match

By contrast, `${i%.avi}.mp4` removes a `.avi` suffix and appends `.mp4`.

`%`, `%%`, `#`, and `##` are shell parameter expansion operators, not regex symbols.

- `%` removes a shortest matching suffix
- `%%` removes the longest matching suffix
- `#` removes a shortest matching prefix
- `##` removes the longest matching prefix

So `${x%% *}` means: from `x`, remove the longest match of ` *` from the end. In practice, it strips everything from the first space onward, leaving the part before the first space.

Example:
`x="hello world test"`
`${x%% *}` → `hello`

In `${1##*.}`, `##` means “remove the longest match from the beginning,” and `*.` means “anything up to the last dot.” So it leaves the part after the final `.` in `$1`.

Examples:
- `name.txt` → `txt`
- `archive.tar.gz` → `gz`
- `noext` → `noext`

So in bash parameter expansion:
- `*` is a wildcard for any string
- `#`/`##` remove from the start
- `%`/`%%` remove from the end

If you want, I can also explain how `%` differs from `#` with examples.

`${1##*.}` is Bash parameter expansion on the script’s first argument.
